title: Blackwell's Island Penitentiary built
summary: A four-story granite prison was built on Blackwell's Island east of Manhattan, originally designed for 800 cells.

citation.quote: Blackwell's Island Penitentiary: Today called Roosevelt Island, this 128-care, two-mile-long island east of Manhattan was home to a granite prison four stories high, built in 1832.

title: The Tombs prison built in New York City
summary: New York City's prison known as the Tombs, modeled after a mausoleum with four distinctive massive columns, was built on a swamp and became notoriously poorly ventilated, overcrowded, and foul.

citation.quote: the Tombs: New York city prison built in 1835, modeled after a mausoleum with four distinctive massive columns.

title: German revolution of 1848
summary: The 1848 revolution in Germany brought radical social ideas to the foreground and laid the basis for expectations that a repressed peasantry and an exploited working class could combine with a new middle class to democratize Germany.

citation.quote: The 1848 revolution brought radical social ideas to the foreground and laid the basis for expectations that a repressed peasantry and an exploited urban working class could combine with a new middle class to create conditions for democratizing Germany.

title: Premiere of Verdi's Il trovatore
summary: Giuseppe Verdi's opera Il trovatore premiered, telling the tragic tale of star-crossed lovers Leonora and the troubador Manrico.

citation.quote: In Giuseppe Verdi's Il trovatore (premiere 1/19/1853), the star-crossed lovers Leonora and the troubador Manrico meet a tragic end.

title: Turgenev publishes Fathers and Sons
summary: Ivan Sergeyevich Turgenev published Fathers and Sons, a love story embedded in timely social issues.

citation.quote: Ivan Sergeyevich Turgenev (1818- 1883) published Fathers and Sons in 1862, a love story embedded in timely, social issues.

title: Dostoyevsky publishes House of the Dead
summary: Fyodor Dostoyevsky published House of the Dead, drawing on his own experiences of imprisonment in czarist Russia for his liberal sympathies.

citation.quote: House of the Dead: Published in 1862 by Fyodor Dostoyevsky. In his work, Dostoyevsky drew upon his own experiences of imprisonment in czarist Russia (1850-54) for his liberal sympathies.

title: Chernyshevsky publishes What Is to Be Done?
summary: Russian intellectual Nikolai Chernyshevsky published the widely influential novel What Is to Be Done?, whose heroine refuses conventional marriage to work, study, and organize cooperative enterprises.

citation.quote: The widely influential novel What Is to Be Done? was published by the Russian intellectual Nikolai Chernyshevsky in 1863.

title: Gontcharov publishes The Precipice
summary: Ivan Alexandrovich Gontcharov published The Precipice (Obriv).

citation.quote: Ivan Alexandrovich Gontcharov (1812-1891) published The Precipice in 1869.

title: Birth of Emma Goldman
summary: June 27 was Emma Goldman's birthday; in 1917 she turned forty-eight, marking twenty-eight years of active struggle against compulsion and injustice.

citation.quote: June 27 happened to be my forty-eighth birthday. It marked twenty-eight years of my life spent in an active struggle against compulsion and injustice.

title: Comstock founds the Society for the Suppression of Vice
summary: American reformer Anthony Comstock founded the Society for the Suppression of Vice and successfully lobbied Congress for the "Comstock" laws banning obscene material from the U.S. mail.

citation.quote: Anthony Comstock (1844-1915): American reformer, founder of the Society for the Suppression of Vice in 1872.

title: Bakunin expelled from the First International
summary: Russian revolutionary and anarchist theorist Michael Bakunin's anti-authoritarian opposition to Karl Marx led to his expulsion from the First International.

citation.quote: Michael Bakunin (1814-1876): Russian revolutionary and anarchist theorist who led anti-authoritarian opposition to Karl Marx, leading to his expulsion from the First International in 1872.

title: Tchaikovsky Circles formed in St. Petersburg
summary: The influential Tchaikovsky Circles were formed in St. Petersburg to unify student revolutionary opposition and to promote political propaganda in the countryside.

citation.quote: Nikolai Tchaikovsky lent his name to the influential Tchaikovsky Circles formed in St. Petersburg in 1872 to unify student revolutionary opposition and then to promote political propaganda in the countryside.

title: Breshkovskaya sentenced to hard labor in Siberia
summary: Russian revolutionary and anarchist Catherine Breshkovskaya was sentenced to twenty years' hard labor in Siberia for revolutionary activities.

citation.quote: Catherine Breshkovskaya (1844-1934): Russian revolutionary, anarchist, and lecturer, sentenced to twenty years' hard labor in Siberia in 1878 for revolutionary activities.

title: Goldman family smuggled from Königsberg to St. Petersburg
summary: Emma, her mother, and two brothers were smuggled across the German-Russian border in deep winter, wading through an icy brook. Emma fell ill afterward, leaving her spine weak for years.

citation.quote: It was in the latter part of 1881 and the winter was particularly severe. The smugglers had told Mother that we would have to wade through deep snow, even across a half-frozen brook.

title: Perovskaya and Zhelyabov executed for assassination of Alexander II
summary: Russian revolutionaries Sophia Perovskaya and Andrei Zhelyabov were executed with their comrades for assassinating Czar Alexander II. Perovskaya was the first woman political prisoner to be executed in Russia.

citation.quote: Sophia Perovskaya (1853-1881) and Andrei Zhelyabov (1850-1881): Russian revolutionary heroes executed with their comrades for the assassination of Czar Alexander II in March 1881.

title: Begins work at glove factory in St. Petersburg
summary: Goldman started working at her father's cousin's glove factory on Vassilevsky Ostrov in St. Petersburg, where six hundred workers labored long hours in dark, unventilated rooms for very small pay.

citation.quote: There were six hundred of us, of all ages, working on costly and beautiful gloves day in, day out, for very small pay. But we were allowed sufficient time for our noon meal and twice a day for tea. We could talk and sing while at work; we were not driven or harassed. That was in St. Petersburg, in 1882.

title: Ibsen publishes An Enemy of the People
summary: Henrik Ibsen published An Enemy of the People, in which a doctor who warns townspeople that local water is contaminated is ostracized for threatening their economic interests.

citation.quote: In An Enemy of the People (1882), a doctor who warns towns-people that local water is contaminated is ostracized for threatening their economic interests.

title: Family moves from Königsberg to St. Petersburg
summary: Emma Goldman, her mother, and her two younger brothers traveled from Königsberg to St. Petersburg to join her father, only to find he had lost his position managing his cousin's dry-goods store.

citation.quote: I had worked in factories before, in St. Petersburg. In the winter of 1882, when Mother, my two little brothers, and I came from Königsberg to join Father in the Russian capital, we found that he had lost his position.

title: Vera Figner arrested
summary: Russian revolutionary Vera Figner, who had joined in the successful conspiracy to assassinate Czar Alexander II, was arrested.

citation.quote: Figner had joined in the successful conspiracy to assassinate Czar Alexander II, for which she was arrested in 1883 and released from Siberia in 1904.

title: Most publishes Science of Revolutionary Warfare
summary: Johann Most's best-known pamphlet, Science of Revolutionary Warfare — a handbook on nitroglycerine, dynamite, bombs, fuses and poisons — was published, cementing the public image of anarchists as bomb throwers.

citation.quote: The best-known pamphlet by anarchist Johann Most was subtitled "A Little Handbook of Instruction in the Use and Preparation of Nitroglycerine, Dynamite ... Bombs, Fuses, Poisons, etc." (1885).

title: Goldman leaves St. Petersburg for America
summary: Goldman and her sister Helena departed St. Petersburg for Hamburg, where they embarked on the steamer Elbe bound for the United States.

citation.quote: Yet how I had fought with my father to get him to let me go to America with Helena! In the end I had won, and late in December 1885, Helena and I had left St. Petersburg for Hamburg, there embarking on the steamer Elbe for the Promised Land.

title: Eight-hour-day labor strikes sweep the country
summary: Labour strikes broke out throughout the United States demanding an eight-hour workday, with Chicago at the center of an increasingly bitter struggle between workers and employers.

citation.quote: She told of the labour strikes that broke out throughout the country in 1886, for the demand of an eight-hour workday. The centre of the movement was Chicago, and there the struggle between the toilers and their bosses became intense and bitter.

title: Goldman family arrives in Rochester
summary: Goldman's father, mother, and brothers Herman and Yegor arrived in Rochester from St. Petersburg, where conditions had become intolerable for Jews and the family grocery business could no longer sustain the bribery needed to remain.

citation.quote: The late fall of 1886 brought the rest of our family to Rochester—Father, Mother, my brothers, Herman and Yegor. Conditions in St. Petersburg had become intolerable for the Jews, and the grocery business did not yield enough for the ever-growing bribery Father had to practise in order to be allowed to exist.

title: Reflection on emigrants to the Promised Land
summary: Travelling steerage again, Goldman reflects on the poor emigrants who, like herself, had pilgrimed to the Promised Land in 1886.

citation.quote: They considered themselves Americans and they were treated accordingly, with more decency than the poor emigrants who had pilgrimed over as I did to the Promised Land in 1886.

title: Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment published
summary: Dostoyevsky's novel Crime and Punishment, an account of man's fall and redemption exploring the existential, moral, and psychological state of the human condition, was published.

citation.quote: Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment: The novel, published in 1886, is an account of man's fall and redemption.

title: Krafft-Ebing publishes Psychopathia Sexualis
summary: German/Austrian psychiatrist Richard Krafft-Ebing authored the widely influential Psychopathia Sexualis.

citation.quote: Richard Krafft-Ebing (1840-1902): German/Austrian psychiatrist, authored widely influential Psychopathia Sexualis (1886).

title: Carpenter publishes Love's Coming of Age
summary: British socialist and poet Edward Carpenter published Love's Coming of Age, advocating sexual liberation for homosexuals and women.

citation.quote: Edward Carpenter (1844-1929): British socialist, writer, and poet; published Love's Coming of Age (1886) advocating sexual liberation for homosexuals and women.

title: Gompers serves as first president of the AFL
summary: English-born Jewish American labor leader Sam Gompers served as the first president of the American Federation of Labor.

citation.quote: Sam Gompers (1850-1924): English-born Jewish American labor leader, first president of the AFL (American Federation of Labor) 1886-1924.

title: Goldman arrives in Rochester, New York
summary: After crossing the Atlantic on the Elbe, Goldman and her sister Helena arrived in Rochester on a cold January morning, met by their sister Lena and Aunt Rachel.

citation.quote: We had heard that Rochester was the “Flower City” of New York, but we arrived there on a bleak and cold January morning. My sister Lena, heavy with her first child, and Aunt Rachel met us.

title: Haymarket Square meeting and bombing
summary: A mass meeting was called in Haymarket Square to protest police violence against McCormick Harvester strikers; addressed by Albert Parsons, August Spies, and Adolph Fischer, it ended when an explosion killed and wounded police officers.

citation.quote: To protest against the outrage a mass meeting was called in Haymarket Square on May 4. It was addressed by Albert Parsons, August Spies, Adolph Fischer, and others, and was quiet and orderly. [ . . . ] Then something flashed through the air and exploded, killing a number of police officers and wounding a score of others.

title: Haymarket martyrs and Goldman's spiritual birth
summary: Goldman credits her spiritual birth as an anarchist to the Chicago martyrs of 1887, executed after the Haymarket affair.

citation.quote: Chicago had been significant in my life. I owed my spiritual birth to the martyrs of 1887.

title: Hearst assumes control of the San Francisco Examiner
summary: Newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst assumed control of the San Francisco Examiner, advocating sensational journalistic practices.

citation.quote: Hearst's Examiner: Newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst (1863-1951) assumed control of the San Francisco Examiner in 1887.

title: Goldman marries Jacob Kershner in Rochester
summary: Emma Goldman married Jacob Kershner in Rochester in a Jewish ceremony performed by a rabbi, which was then legally sufficient. Their marriage proved troubled from the wedding night, when Kershner revealed his impotence.

citation.quote: In February 1887 we were married in Rochester by a rabbi, according to Jewish rites, which were then considered sufficient by the law of the country.

title: Execution of the Haymarket anarchists
summary: Albert Parsons, August Spies, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel were hanged in Chicago on the day Goldman would later call Black Friday; Louis Lingg had died earlier and others received prison sentences.

citation.quote: Twenty-one months had passed since the Black Friday of November 11, when the Chicago men had suffered their martyrdom, yet every detail stood out clear before my vision and affected me as if it had happened but yesterday.

title: Execution of the Chicago Haymarket martyrs
summary: The Chicago anarchists were executed, an event whose twenty-fifth anniversary Goldman commemorated in 1912 and which she described as the most decisive influence in her existence.

citation.quote: November II, 1887—November 11, 1912! Twenty-five years, an infinitesimal fraction of time in the upward march of the race, but an eternity for him who dies many deaths in the course of his life.

title: Execution of the Haymarket martyrs in Chicago
summary: Goldman recalls that November 10 had been the last day on earth of her comrades martyred in Chicago twenty-seven years before her 1914 lecture, evoking August Spies's final prophecy that their silence would be more powerful than the voices strangled that day.

citation.quote: It had been the last day on earth of my comrades martyred in Chicago twenty-seven years before... The vision of our precious dead was before me, bearing witness to the last prophecy of August Spies: "Our silence will be more powerful than the voices you strangle today." In 1887 Chicago's sole answer to anarchism was the gallows; in 1914 it was eagerly listening to the ideas for which Parsons and his comrades had died.

title: Haymarket martyrs executed
summary: The Haymarket martyrs were executed in Chicago.

citation.quote: anniversary of the 11th of November: On November 11, 1887, the Haymarket martyrs were executed in Chicago.

title: Yakutsk prison massacre of political prisoners
summary: Russian political prisoners in Yakutsk who had protested the maltreatment of their comrades were lured into the prison yard and fired upon by guards; several were killed, including women, and others were subsequently hanged.

citation.quote: A year before, fearful things had taken place in Yakutsk. Politicals who had protested against the maltreatment of their comrades were lured into the prison yard and fired upon by guards; a number of prisoners were killed, among them women, while several others were subsequently hanged in the prison for "inciting an outbreak."

title: Paris International Socialist Congress declares May Day
summary: The International Socialist Congress held in Paris decided to turn the first of May into a worldwide holiday of labour, an idea that caught the imagination of progressive workers everywhere.

citation.quote: At the International Socialist Congress held in Paris in 1889 the decision had been made to turn the first of May into a worldwide holiday of labour.

title: Goldman's arrival in New York
summary: Goldman recalls her arrival in New York in 1889 as a poor, inexperienced child alone in the American metropolis, contrasting it with her 1895 departure as an experienced public figure.

citation.quote: My departure was quite different from my arrival in New York in 1889. I was very poor then, poor in more than merely material things. I was a child, inexperienced and alone in the whirlpool of the American metropolis.

title: Goldman first arrives in New York
summary: Goldman reflects that she counted her real birth from 1889, when, as a girl of twenty, she had first come to New York.

citation.quote: While at liberty I had hardly noticed age creeping up, perhaps because I had counted my real birth from 1889, when, as a girl of twenty, I had first come to New York.

title: Jane Addams founds Hull House
summary: American reformer Jane Addams founded Hull House, a settlement house in Chicago's Near West Side that provided services including a kindergarten, employment bureau, art gallery, libraries, and classes in music and art.

citation.quote: Hull House: founded in 1889 by American reformer Jane Addams (1860-1935). Located in Chicago's Near West Side, the settlement house provided services for the neighborhood such as a kindergarten and day-care facilities...

title: Goldman arrives in New York City
summary: Emma Goldman, age twenty, arrived in New York City via the West Shore train from Rochester and ferry from Weehawken, carrying five dollars, a hand-bag, and three addresses.

citation.quote: It was the 15th of August 1889, the day of my arrival in New York City. I was twenty years old.

title: Goldman first hears Johann Most speak
summary: On her first day in New York, Goldman attended a lecture by Johann Most, whose scorching denunciation of American conditions and tribute to the Haymarket martyrs stirred her profoundly.

citation.quote: His speech was a scorching denunciation of American conditions, a biting satire on the injustice and brutality of the dominant powers, a passionate tirade against those responsible for the Haymarket tragedy and the execution of the Chicago anarchists in November 1887.

title: Joseph Peukert immigrates to America
summary: Bohemian-born anarchist Joseph Peukert, founder of Gruppe Autonomie in London and an advocate of decentralized organization and propaganda by the deed, immigrated to America.

citation.quote: Immigrated in 1890 to America, where he worked to clear his name of Johann Most's charge that he had acted as a political spy...

title: Sanborn publishes biography of Thoreau
summary: Frank B. Sanborn's biography of American essayist and reformer Henry David Thoreau was published.

citation.quote: Frank B. Sanborn (1831-1917): His biography of American essayist, transcendentalist, and reformer Henry David Thoreau (1817-1862) was published in 1890.

title: George Kennan's Siberia expose stirs radical ranks
summary: Reports brought from Siberia by American journalist George Kennan about Russian political prisoners and exiles moved the American press and aroused East Side radicals.

citation.quote: In the winter of that year (1890) the radical ranks were aroused over the report brought from Siberia by George Kennan, an American journalist. His account of the harrowing conditions of the Russian political prisoners and exiles moved even the American press to lengthy comments.

title: Canvassing New England farmers for crayon portraits
summary: Goldman recalls that in 1891 she and Sasha canvassed New England farmers, selling crayon portraits, finding them inhospitable and close-fisted.

citation.quote: I found him just as inhospitable and close-fisted as the farmers Sasha and I had canvassed for crayon portraits in 1891.

title: Goldman speaks from a truck at Union Square May Day rally
summary: At the New York May Day demonstration in Union Square, after socialist organizers refused the anarchists a platform, Goldman was lifted onto a socialist truck and continued speaking even as the owner drove the wagon away.

citation.quote: In this year, 1891, the decision of the Congress was to find wide application. On the first of May the toilers were to lay down their tools, stop their machines, leave the factories and mines.

title: Goldman begins lecturing in Chicago
summary: Goldman notes she had been lecturing in Chicago since 1892, but only on this 1910 visit realized the city's full possibilities for her work.

citation.quote: I had been lecturing in the city on Lake Michigan since 1892, but it was only on this visit that I realized its possibilities.

title: Berkman's departure for Pittsburgh recalled
summary: Goldman recalls that since Berkman had gone to Pittsburgh in 1892 (for the attempt on Frick), she had endured many police raids but had managed to rescue copies of his clandestinely-published prison writings, 'The Prison Blossoms.'

citation.quote: Notwithstanding the many police raids I had suffered since Sasha had gone to Pittsburgh in 1892, I had managed to rescue some copies of "The Prison Blossoms," which he had published *sub rosa* in the penitentiary.

title: Solidarity published in New York
summary: Solidarity, the first English-language anarchist paper in New York, was published; Goldman helped support the paper financially.

citation.quote: Solidarity (1892-1898): first English-language anarchist paper in New York. EG also helped to support the paper financially.

title: Homestead lockout begins between Carnegie Steel and Amalgamated Association
summary: Trouble broke out between the Carnegie Steel Company and its employees in the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers, with Henry Clay Frick taking charge while Andrew Carnegie was away.

citation.quote: It was May 1892. News from Pittsburgh announced that trouble had broken out between the Carnegie Steel Company and its employees organized in the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers.

title: Pinkertons fire on Homestead steel-workers from barge on Monongahela
summary: A barge of strike-breakers and armed Pinkertons attempting to land at the fortified Homestead mills opened fire on steel-workers along the Monongahela River, killing several including a boy and wounding scores.

citation.quote: A few days after our return to New York the news was flashed across the country of the slaughter of steel-workers by Pinkertons. Frick had fortified the Homestead mills, built a high fence around them. Then, in the dead of night, a barge packed with strike-breakers, under protection of heavily armed Pinkerton thugs, quietly stole up the Monongahela River.

title: Reflection on the black day of July 1892
summary: Goldman recalls the haunting impact of the events of July 1892 (Berkman's attentat against Frick) on her life ever since, while grieving over Sasha's prolonged imprisonment.

citation.quote: Could I explain what those years had been to me, ever since that black day in July 1892. Life is inexorable; it does not let you pause at any point.

title: Berkman's Attentat on Henry Clay Frick
summary: Goldman referred back to the heroic moment of July 1892 in which Alexander Berkman carried out his Attentat, the act that led to his fourteen-year imprisonment and inspired Prison Memoirs.

citation.quote: I felt outraged by the man's denouncing the Attentat on the occasion of the birth of Sasha's book, a work conceived in that heroic moment of July 1892 and nourished by tears and blood throughout the dark and terrible years that followed.

title: Goldman recalls bomb-making with Berkman in Peppi's flat
summary: Goldman relives the week she spent watching Sasha (Berkman) experiment with a bomb in her room in Peppi's flat on Fifth Street, an act she had justified at the time by the belief that the end justifies the means.

citation.quote: In my mind I saw my little room in Peppi's flat, on Fifth Street, its window-blinds drawn, Sasha experimenting with a bomb, and me watching. I had silenced my fear for the tenants, in case of an accident, by repeating to myself that the end justified the means. With accusing clarity I now relived that nerve-racking week in July 1892.

title: Goldman parts from Berkman at New York train station
summary: Goldman recalls the moment she parted from Alexander Berkman at the Baltimore and Ohio Station in New York as he left to carry out his attentat against Henry Clay Frick.

citation.quote: Out of my depths suddenly rose the past. It was July 10, 1892, and I saw myself at the Baltimore and Ohio Station in New York, standing on the steps of a moving train, clinging to Sasha.

title: Goldman attempts to solicit on Fourteenth Street to raise money for Berkman
summary: Goldman walked Fourteenth Street as a prostitute to raise money for Berkman's planned attentat against Frick; a stranger gave her ten dollars and sent her home, recognizing she was not suited to the work.

citation.quote: Saturday evening, July 16, 1892, I walked up and down Fourteenth Street, one of the long procession of girls I had so often seen plying their trade.

title: Newspapers report Berkman's attempt on Frick
summary: On Saturday, July 23, Fedya brought Goldman a newspaper announcing that Alexander Berkman had shot Henry Clay Frick and been overpowered by working-men after a desperate struggle.

citation.quote: In the early afternoon of Saturday, July 23, Fedya rushed into my room with a newspaper. There it was, in large black letters: “YOUNG MAN BY THE NAME OF ALEXANDER BERGMAN SHOOTS FRICK—ASSASSIN OVERPOWERED BY WORKING-MEN AFTER DESPERATE STRUGGLE.”

title: Most publishes "Attentats-Reflexionen" in Freiheit
summary: Johann Most published "Attentats-Reflexionen (Reflections on Propaganda by Deed)" in the Freiheit, repudiating the very tactics of violent revolt he had long advocated.

citation.quote: Then came Most’s article “Attentats-Reflexionen (Reflections on Propaganda by Deed)” in the Freiheit of August 27, which was a complete reversal of everything that Most had till then persistently advocated.

title: Berkman sentenced to twenty-two years
summary: Goldman recalls the September 1892 trial day when the judge added an extra year to Berkman's twenty-one-year sentence, calling the judge barbarous.

citation.quote: The judge who had added the extra year to the inhuman sentence of twenty-one now appeared more barbarous than on that trial day in September 1892.

title: Berkman sentenced to twenty-two years in prison
summary: While Goldman was about to speak in Baltimore on Monday the 19th, a telegram informed her that Alexander Berkman's trial had taken place that day and he had been sentenced to twenty-two years in prison.

citation.quote: In the second week of September I was invited to speak in Baltimore, my lecture being scheduled for Monday, the 19th. As I was about to ascend the platform, a telegram was handed to me. The trial had taken place that very day and Sasha had been condemned to twenty-two years in prison!

title: Alexander Berkman tried and sentenced to 22 years
summary: Berkman was abruptly brought to trial on six indictments stemming from his attack on Frick, denied effective interpretation, and convicted by a jury without deliberation. Judge McClung sentenced him to 21 years in the Western Penitentiary plus one year in the Allegheny County Workhouse.

citation.quote: On the morning of the 19th he was suddenly ordered to get ready. He had barely time to gather up the sheets of his speech. Strange and antagonistic faces met him in the court-room.

title: Berkman writes Goldman about a possible visit
summary: In early November, Berkman sent word that he might be granted a prison visit and asked Goldman to arrange for his sister from Russia to come — a coded request that she impersonate the sister.

citation.quote: Early in November came the first sign of Sasha’s reawakened interest in life. His letter informed me that he might have the privilege of a visitor.

title: Goldman's last permitted visit to Berkman in prison
summary: Goldman recalls that since her visit to Sasha (Alexander Berkman) in November 1892, he had not again been permitted to see anyone in the Allegheny prison.

citation.quote: The Inspector had kept his promise; since my visit in November 1892, Sasha had not again been permitted to see anyone.

title: Goldman visits Berkman in Western Penitentiary as 'Mrs. Niedermann'
summary: Posing as Berkman's married sister Mrs. E. Niedermann, Goldman arrived in Pittsburgh on Thanksgiving Day and used a pass from the Chief Prison Inspector to visit Berkman in the Western Penitentiary. During the brief, guarded meeting he secretly passed her a note via a kiss.

citation.quote: It contained a pass from the Chief Prison Inspector of the Western Penitentiary for Mrs. E. Niedermann, sister of Prisoner A-7, for a visit on the 26th of November.

title: Goldman confronts Inspector Reed after being unmasked
summary: Returning to jeweler-inspector Reed's shop the day after her prison visit to obtain a second pass, Goldman was denounced as Berkman's mistress. She swept Reed's merchandise to the floor and threatened him before being forced out.

citation.quote: I went to Reed’s store the next day. I looked shabby in my threadbare coat amid the sparkling jewellery, silver, and gold.

title: Union Square demonstration
summary: Goldman recalls the Union Square demonstration of 1893 as the only previous occasion when she had seen masses as eager and enthusiastic as those drawn to her San Francisco lectures.

citation.quote: Never in all the years since I had first gone on tour, with the exception of the Union Square demonstration in 1893, had I seen masses so eager and enthusiastic.

title: Governor Altgeld pardons surviving Haymarket prisoners
summary: Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three surviving Haymarket prisoners — Samuel Fielden, Oscar Neebe, and Michael Schwab — exposing the miscarriage of justice in the state's original prosecution.

citation.quote: Governor John Peter Altgeld (1847-1902.): governor of Illinois (1893-97), pardoned the three surviving Haymarket prisoners Samuel Fielden, Oscar Neebe, and Michael Schwab on June 26, 1893.

title: Union Square unemployed demonstration
summary: Goldman recalls a prior demonstration for the unemployed held at Union Square in August 1893, comparing it to the present mass meeting for the jobless.

citation.quote: The mass meeting was large and spirited; it reminded me of a similar event in the same place and for the same purpose, the demonstration of August 1893.

title: Goldman visits Rochester after prison release
summary: Goldman made a brief visit to Rochester after her release from prison, her first time back since before her imprisonment, and saw her father for the first time in five years.

citation.quote: During my short stay in Rochester in 1894, I had seen my father for the first time in five years. I still felt estranged, but no longer so hostile.

title: Goldman awakens deeper feeling in her brother Yegor
summary: On her 1894 visit to Rochester, Goldman seemed to awaken a deeper feeling in her brother Yegor, who declared her his heroine and asked her to persuade their father to let him go to New York to study.

citation.quote: But on my visit in 1894 I seemed to awaken a deeper feeling in him.

title: Darrow defends Debs in the Pullman strike
summary: American lawyer Clarence Darrow achieved national recognition defending Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union during the Pullman strike.

citation.quote: He achieved national recognition defending Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union during the 1894 Pullman strike.

title: Caserio assassinates French President Sadi Carnot
summary: Italian anarchist Santa Caserio assassinated Sadi Carnot, president of France.

citation.quote: Santa Caserio (1873-1894): Italian anarchist and assassin of Sadi Carnot, president of France, June 24, 1894.

title: Goldman's first visit to England
summary: Goldman recalls her earlier 1895 visit to England, which had taught her about the pride Englishmen take in their traditions.

citation.quote: My visit in 1895 and my experiences this time had taught me to know the pride of Englishmen in their traditions.

title: Sails for England
summary: Six years to the day after her new life in New York had begun, Goldman sailed steerage for England to embark on a lecture tour and to study midwifery and nursing in Vienna.

citation.quote: On the 15th of August 1895, exactly six years since my new life in New York had begun, I sailed for England.

title: Day trip to Manhattan Beach with Ed
summary: About a fortnight after her release from prison, Goldman and Ed spent a day together at Manhattan Beach, where Ed urged her to give up the platform and pressed his view that she was a born mother.

citation.quote: I had been out of prison about a fortnight and we had not yet had one complete day alone. We went to Manhattan Beach. The November air was sharp, the sea stormy; but the sun shone brightly.

title: Goldman's first visit to Paris
summary: Four years before her 1900 trip, Goldman had briefly visited Paris on her way from Vienna, staying with German anarchists in a suburb and seeing little of the city.

citation.quote: Four years previously, in 1896, I had visited the city on my way from Vienna. That experience had been a great disappointment.

title: John Turner's first American lecture tour
summary: British anarchist John Turner first came to the United States and lectured extensively for seven months.

citation.quote: Meanwhile John Turner had announced his coming to the States. He had been in America in 1896 and had lectured extensively during seven months.

title: Bryan proposes unlimited coinage of silver
summary: American political leader William Jennings Bryan proposed unlimited coinage of silver as a remedy to the economic ills afflicting farmers and industrial workers.

citation.quote: William Jennings Bryan (1860-1925): American political leader and reformer. In 1896 Bryan proposed unlimited coinage of silver as a remedy to the economic ills afflicting farmers and industrial workers.

title: Baginski publishes Die Sturmglocken
summary: German American anarchist editor Max Baginski published the journal Die Sturmglocken.

citation.quote: Max Baginski (1864-1943): German American anarchist and editor, publisher of the journal Die Sturmglocken in 1896.

title: Goldman's earlier tour of Pennsylvania mining region
summary: Goldman recalled traveling through the Pennsylvania coal-mining region in 1897, used as a point of comparison to the worse conditions she found on her later visit.

citation.quote: In Pennsylvania I found the condition of the miners since the “settlement” of the strike worse than in 1897 when I had gone through the region.

title: Goldman meets Max Baginski in Chicago
summary: Ten years after the 1887 martyrs, Goldman found Max in Chicago, whose understanding and tender companionship would inspire and sustain her through the years.

citation.quote: Ten years later I found Max there, whose understanding and tender companionship had not ceased to inspire and sustain me through the years.

title: Goldman first meets Jack London in California
summary: Goldman first met Jack London among young socialist students at the Strunskys' home during her first visit to California in 1897.

citation.quote: I had met him with other young socialist students at the Strunskys' on my first visit to California, in 1897.

title: Havelock Ellis publishes Sexual Inversion
summary: British doctor and sexual psychologist Havelock Ellis published Sexual Inversion, one of the first scientific books not to treat homosexuality as a pathological condition.

citation.quote: His Sexual Inversion (1897) was one of the first scientific books not to treat homosexuality as a pathological condition.

title: Abe Isaak publishes Free Society
summary: Russian-born American anarchist Abe Isaak published Free Society, a San Francisco-based anarchist journal that became the most prominent English-language anarchist journal in the United States at the beginning of the 20th century.

citation.quote: Free Society (1897-1901): San Francisco-based anarchist journal published by Abe Isaak. Most prominent English-language anarchist journal in the United States at the beginning of the 20th century.

title: Angiolillo assassinates Spanish prime minister
summary: Italian anarchist Michele Angiolillo assassinated the prime minister of Spain.

citation.quote: Bresci's, Angiolillo's: the Italian anarchists Michele Angiolillo and Gaetano Bresci were the assassins of the prime minister of Spain (August 1897) and King Umberto of Italy (July 1900), respectively.

title: Kropotkin's lecture tour of the United States
summary: Peter Kropotkin visited the States on a successful lecture tour, the proceeds of which helped revive the anarchist paper Solidarity and reinvigorate the American movement.

citation.quote: Peter had visited the States in 1898, but I was at the time on the Coast and unable to attend his lectures. I knew, however, that his tour had been very successful and that he had left a most gratifying impression. The proceeds of his meetings had helped to revive Solidarity and inject new life into our movement.

title: Goldman and Baginski become lovers
summary: Emma Goldman and Max Baginski, who first met in Philadelphia in 1893, became lovers.

citation.quote: He met EG in Philadelphia in 1893; they became lovers in 1898.

title: The Boer War
summary: Britain engaged Dutch settlers in South Africa, seeking to extend its imperial reach over the gold mines of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. After an initial success, two years of guerrilla warfare ensued until the Boer resistance was brutally put down.

citation.quote: In their military engagement with the Dutch settlers in South Africa (the Boer War, 1899-1902.), Britain sought to extend its imperial reach over the rich gold mines of the Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State.

title: Paris Exposition prompts plans for anarchist congress
summary: The Paris Exposition planned for 1900 inspired European anarchists to organize a congress around the same time, taking advantage of reduced fares to bring comrades from different countries.

citation.quote: The Paris Exposition, which was being planned for 1900, suggested the idea to our European comrades of holding an anarchist congress at about the same time. There would be reduced fares, and many of our friends would be able to come from different countries.

title: Anti-war meeting at South Place Institute during Boer War
summary: Goldman addressed an anti-Anglo-Boer War meeting at South Place Institute in London, chaired alongside Tom Mann, winning over a hostile patriotic crowd with appeals to English literary tradition.

citation.quote: On the appointed day, accompanied by my escort, I reached South Place Institute a few hours before the crowd began to gather. Very soon the hall was filled. When Tom Mann stepped on to the platform, there was loud booing, which drowned the applause of our friends.

title: Neo-Malthusian Conference in Paris
summary: Goldman attended the Neo-Malthusian Conference held in Paris, after which she added birth-control to her lecture series.

citation.quote: After my return from the Neo-Malthusian Conference, held in Paris in 1900, I had added to my lecture series the subject of birth-control.

title: Goldman's earlier visit to London
summary: Goldman recalls her previous visit to London in 1900, when she had lived in a basement, contrasting it with her current quarters on the heights at the home of Doris Zhook.

citation.quote: Unlike my visit in 1900, when I lived in a basement, my quarters this time were on the heights: a bedroom on the third floor in the house of my old friend Doris Zhook.

title: Whitman's Song of the Open Road first published
summary: Walt Whitman's poem "The Song of the Open Road" was first published in Leaves of Grass.

citation.quote: The Open Road: "The Song of the Open Road," by the American poet Walt Whitman (1819-1892), was first published in Leaves of Grass in 1900.

title: Goldman and Havel arrive in Paris
summary: Goldman departed England for Paris with Hippolyte Havel, arriving on a drizzling January morning and stopping at a hotel on Boulevard Saint-Michel to prepare for the anarchist congress.

citation.quote: I departed from England for Paris, together with Hippolyte, arriving in that city on a drizzling January morning and stopping in a hotel on Boulevard Saint-Michel.

title: Bresci assassinates King Umberto of Italy
summary: Italian anarchist Gaetano Bresci assassinated King Umberto of Italy.

citation.quote: Bresci's, Angiolillo's: the Italian anarchists Michele Angiolillo and Gaetano Bresci were the assassins of the prime minister of Spain (August 1897) and King Umberto of Italy (July 1900), respectively.

title: Goldman visits Berkman at Western Penitentiary
summary: After nine years since their last fleeting meeting in November 1892, Goldman visited Alexander Berkman at the Western Penitentiary; he sat mute, fumbling with her watch-chain, his face grey and changed.

citation.quote: Once more I stood within the prison walls of the Western Penitentiary, with fast-beating heart straining to catch the sound of Sasha's step. Nine years had passed since that November day in 1892 when for a fleeting moment I had been brought face to face with him, only again to be wrenched away—nine years replete with the torment of endless time.

title: Goldman released after Buffalo extradition fails
summary: After Buffalo authorities again failed to produce evidence connecting Goldman to Czolgosz's act, a Chicago judge set her free following a two-hour courtroom argument.

citation.quote: Again I was taken to court for a hearing and again the Buffalo authorities failed to produce evidence to connect me with Czolgosz's act. The Buffalo representative and the Chicago judge sitting on the case kept up a verbal fight for two hours, at the end of which Buffalo was robbed of its prey. I was set free.

title: Johann Most arrested for republishing Heinzen essay
summary: Johann Most was arrested in New York for an article in the Freiheit reproducing Karl Heinzen's essay on political violence, amid the post-McKinley crackdown on anarchists.

citation.quote: Johann Most was arrested for an article in the Freiheit reproducing an essay on political violence by Karl Heinzen, the famous '48 revolutionist, then dead many years. Most was out on bail awaiting his trial.

title: Harry Gordon nearly lynched in Pittsburgh
summary: In the wave of anti-anarchist violence following McKinley's assassination, Harry Gordon was dragged into the street in Pittsburgh with a rope around his neck, saved only by bystanders moved by his wife and children's pleas.

citation.quote: In Pittsburgh our good friend Harry Gordon was dragged out into the street and nearly lynched. A rope already around his neck, he was saved at the last moment by some bystanders who were touched by the pleading of Mrs. Gordon and her two children.

title: Mob attacks Freie Arbeiter Stimme office in New York
summary: A mob attacked the office of the Yiddish anarchist paper Freie Arbeiter Stimme in New York, smashing furniture and destroying type, with no police intervention.

citation.quote: In New York the office of the Freie Arbeiter Stimme was attacked by a mob, the furniture demolished, and the type destroyed. In no case did the police interfere with the doings of the patriotic ruffians.

title: Goldman brought close to death over Czolgosz stance
summary: In Chicago in 1901, Goldman was brought close to death because of her sympathetic attitude toward Leon Czolgosz, the assassin of President McKinley.

citation.quote: It was also in Chicago, in 1901, that I had been brought close to death because of my attitude towards Leon Czolgosz, and was it not Chicago that had given me Ben?

title: Kropotkin lectures at Grand Central Palace
summary: Peter Kropotkin spoke to a packed audience at Grand Central Palace in New York on the first Sunday afternoon in May, during his American tour for the Lowell Institute on Ideals in Russian Literature.

citation.quote: From all parts of the city people came streaming in to Grand Central Palace to hear Peter Kropotkin on the first Sunday afternoon in May. For once even the papers were decent: they could not gainsay the man's charm, the power of his intellect, the simplicity and logic of his delivery and argumentation.

title: Goldman lectures in Cleveland, first meets Czolgosz
summary: Goldman delivered a lecture on Anarchism before the Franklin Liberal Club in Cleveland, where she first encountered a young man with golden hair who asked her for reading recommendations — later identified as Leon Czolgosz.

citation.quote: The subject of my lecture in Cleveland, early in May of that year, was Anarchism, delivered before the Franklin Liberal Club, a radical organization. During the intermission before the discussion I noticed a man looking over the titles of the pamphlets and books on sale near the platform.

title: Berkman writes from prison hospital after strait jacket
summary: Alexander Berkman sent a sub rosa letter from the Western Penitentiary hospital describing being kept in a strait jacket for eight days after over a year in solitary confinement, and the death of his friend Russell.

citation.quote: On our return to Rochester I found two letters from Sasha. The first, sub rosa, dated July 10, had evidently been delayed in transmission.

title: Czolgosz visits Goldman in Chicago
summary: A young man calling himself Nieman — later identified as Leon Czolgosz — visited Goldman at the Isaak home in Chicago and accompanied her to the station as she departed for Rochester.

citation.quote: I knew I had not been with Czolgosz except for a few minutes in Cleveland on May 5, and for half an hour in Chicago on July 12.

title: Berkman's sentence commuted under new law
summary: Berkman wrote to Goldman that a new commutation law had reduced his sentence by 2½ years, his privileges had been restored by a new Inspector, and he had been allowed his first visit from a comrade — Harry Gordon — in nine years.

citation.quote: Direct to Box A 7. Allegheny City, Pa. July 25, 1901.

title: Death of President McKinley announced to Goldman in jail
summary: While imprisoned in the Cook County Jail, Goldman was informed by detectives and reporters that President McKinley had died from the wounds inflicted by Czolgosz.

citation.quote: One evening, while engrossed in a book, I was surprised by several detectives and reporters. "The President has just died," they announced. "How do you feel about it? Aren't you sorry?"

title: Czolgosz shoots President McKinley at Pan-American Exposition
summary: While Goldman was in St. Louis canvassing stationery stores for orders, newsboys cried that President McKinley had been shot at the Exposition grounds in Buffalo by a young man named Leon Czolgosz.

citation.quote: The following day, September 6, I canvassed every important stationery and novelty store in St. Louis for orders for Ed's firm, but I failed to interest anyone in my samples... As I stood at a street-corner wearily waiting for a car, I heard a newsboy cry: "Extra! Extra! President McKinley shot!"

title: Daily News reporter spreads Czolgosz-Goldman story
summary: Hippolyte recounts that a Daily News reporter came to the Isaak home in Chicago seeking information about Czolgosz, which Isaak provided, sparking the fabricated story linking Goldman to the assassination.

citation.quote: The whole dastardly story was started by a Daily News reporter who used to hang round here pretending to sympathize with our ideas. Late in the afternoon of September 6 he came to the house. He wanted to know all about a certain Czolgosz or Nieman.

title: Czolgosz assassinates President McKinley
summary: American self-proclaimed anarchist Leon Czolgosz assassinated President William McKinley.

citation.quote: Leon Czolgosz (1873-1901): American self-proclaimed anarchist and assassin of President McKinley (September 6, 1901).

title: Goldman arrested in Chicago after McKinley shooting
summary: Detectives led by Captain Schuettler raided the apartment where Goldman was hiding and arrested her; she was subjected to the third degree at police headquarters from 10:30 a.m. until 7 p.m.

citation.quote: I had been arrested a number of times since 1893; no violence, however, had ever been practised on me. On the day of my arrest, which was September 10, I was kept at police headquarters in a stifling room and grilled to exhaustion from 10.30 a.m. till 7 p.m.

title: Execution of Leon Czolgosz at Auburn Prison
summary: Leon Czolgosz was executed in the electric chair at Auburn Prison. Before dying he denied that Emma Goldman had any role in his act, saying he did it alone for the American people.

citation.quote: The last act was staged in Auburn Prison. It was early dawn, October 29, 1901. The condemned man sat strapped to the electric chair.

title: Berkman writes sub rosa letter on Czolgosz's act
summary: Alexander Berkman writes a long sub rosa letter from prison reflecting on Goldman's visit and arguing that Leon Czolgosz's assassination of McKinley lacked the social necessity required to make an Attentat educational.

citation.quote: It was a long *sub rosa* letter, dated December 20 and written on several slips of paper in the very small script Sasha had acquired, each word standing out clear and distinct.

title: Letter arrives from Sasha Berkman
summary: Goldman receives a long sub rosa letter from Alexander Berkman, dated December 20, addressing the McKinley assassination and Czolgosz's act. The letter reveals Berkman's view that Czolgosz's deed lacked social necessity.

citation.quote: At last, on December 31, a letter arrived from him. No greater New Year's gift could have come to me.

title: Goldman visits Czolgosz's family in Cleveland
summary: Goldman visited Cleveland to learn about Leon Czolgosz, meeting his parents and sister and gathering details of his impoverished and isolated childhood.

citation.quote: What Miss T. told me bore out all that I had guessed and what I had learned about Leon in 1902 when I visited Cleveland. I had hunted up his parents; they were dark people, the father hardened by toil, the stepmother with a dull, vacant look.

title: Goldman moves into 210 East Thirteenth Street
summary: Goldman first moved into 210 East Thirteenth Street in New York to share a flat with the Horrs, becoming one of the first tenants of the newly built house that would serve as her home and Mother Earth office for a decade.

citation.quote: When I had first moved into 210 East Thirteenth Street, in 1903, to share the flat with the Horrs, we were the first tenants in the recently built house.

title: Kushnev pogrom inspires Byalek's City of Slaughter
summary: Chaim Nachman Byalek's Hebrew poem "The City of Slaughter" was inspired by the Kushnev pogrom of 1903.

citation.quote: Chaim Nachman Byalek (1873-1934): achieved international recognition with the publication of "The City of Slaughter," a Hebrew poem inspired by the Kushnev pogrom of 1903.

title: Federal Anti-Anarchist Law passed by Congress
summary: Congress passed the Federal Anti-Anarchist Law, under which John Turner was the first to be arrested and threatened with deportation.

citation.quote: Turner was given the honour of being the first to fall under the ban of the Federal Anti-Anarchist Law passed by Congress on March 3, 1903.

title: Goldman's common work with Breshkovskaya
summary: Goldman first came to love Catherine Breshkovskaya (Babushka) through their common revolutionary work in America during 1904 and 1905, when Breshkovskaya toured to raise support.

citation.quote: Her simple grandeur, the charm and beauty of her personality, which I had learned to love during our common work in 1904 and 1905, had too deeply impressed me for me to give Babushka up so easily.

title: Goldman rents apartment at 210 East Thirteenth Street
summary: Emma Goldman rented part of an apartment at 210 East Thirteenth Street, which remained her home for ten years.

citation.quote: In 1904 EG had rented part of an apartment at 210 East Thirteenth Street, which remained her home for ten years (see LML, 1970, 349-50).

title: Vera Figner released from Siberia
summary: Russian revolutionary Vera Figner was released from Siberia, where she had been since her 1883 arrest for participation in the assassination of Czar Alexander II.

citation.quote: Figner had joined in the successful conspiracy to assassinate Czar Alexander II, for which she was arrested in 1883 and released from Siberia in 1904.

title: Orleneff and Nazimova arrive in America
summary: Pavel Orleneff and Mme Nazimova came to America in early 1905, taking the East Side by storm with their production of Tchirikov's The Chosen People as a protest against the pogroms sweeping Russia.

citation.quote: Pavel Nikolayevitch Orleneff and Mme Nazimova had come to America in the early part of 1905, taking the East Side by storm with their wonderful production of Tchirikov's The Chosen People.

title: Assassinations of Grand Duke Sergius and Shipiaghin
summary: Kalayev and Balmashov, members of the Fighting Organization of the Social Revolutionary Party, killed Grand Duke Sergius and Shipiaghin in retaliation for the January 22 massacre.

citation.quote: Kalayev and Balmashov, members of the Fighting Organization of the Social Revolutionary Party, had taken the lives of Grand Duke Sergius and Shipiaghin in retaliation for the butchery of January 22.

title: General strike across Russia
summary: The assassinations were followed by a general strike throughout Russia involving every stratum of society, including prostitutes who joined the masses.

citation.quote: Those acts had been followed by a general strike throughout the length and breadth of Russia, participated in by large sections from every stratum in society.

title: Russian Revolution of 1905 invoked at London dinner
summary: At her welcome dinner in London, Goldman reminded her audience of the Russian Revolution of 1905 and the horrors that followed it as background for her opposition to Soviet repression.

citation.quote: I reminded my hearers of the Russian Revolution of 1905 and the horrors that followed it.

title: Breshkovskaya departs on American lecture tour
summary: In January, Catherine Breshkovskaya went on a lecture tour, allowing Goldman to turn to other interests and reunite with her niece Stella.

citation.quote: In January Babushka went on a lecture tour, and I could turn to other interests and activities.

title: Russian New Year's ball welcomes 1905 with Babushka
summary: At the Russian New Year's ball Goldman and comrades greeted the advent of 1905, with Catherine Breshkovskaya dancing the kazatchok.

citation.quote: At the Russian New Year's ball we greeted the advent of 1905 standing in a circle, Babushka dancing the kazatchok with one of the boys.

title: Bloody Sunday massacre at the Winter Palace
summary: Thousands led by Father Gapon assembled before the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg to appeal to the Tsar for relief and were massacred by the autocrat's troops.

citation.quote: Our strenuous work for Russia at this time received additional significance by the news of the appalling tragedy of January 22 in St. Petersburg. Thousands of people, led by Father Gapon, assembled before the Winter Palace to appeal to the Tsar for relief, had been brutally mowed down, massacred in cold blood by the autocrat's henchmen.

title: Massacre in front of the Winter Palace
summary: The slaughter of demonstrators outside the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg set off a chain of tremendous events that preceded the October revolution.

citation.quote: Kalayev and Balmashov, members of the Fighting Organization of the Social Revolutionary Party, had taken the lives of Grand Duke Sergius and Shipiaghin in retaliation for the butchery of January 22.

title: Important events in the 1905 Russian revolution
summary: Important events in the 1905 revolution in Russia occurred in March.

citation.quote: the historic revolutionary month of March: Important events in the 1905 revolution in Russia occurred in March.

title: Goldman reflects on Sasha's thirteen years imprisoned
summary: In July 1905, Goldman reflected that thirteen years earlier Alexander Berkman had left to stake his life for the cause, and that his penitentiary term was ending though he still had to serve a year in the workhouse.

citation.quote: It was the month of July 1905. Just thirteen years before, he had left me to stake his life for our cause. His Calvary was soon to end, but only to continue in another place; he still had to serve another year in the workhouse.

title: Berkman's last day in the penitentiary
summary: Berkman sent his final note from the penitentiary on Wednesday the 19th, marking his last hours within the prison walls before transfer to the workhouse.

citation.quote: It's Wednesday morning, the 19th, at last!

title: Russian Revolution of October 1905
summary: News of the Russian revolution reached Goldman and her comrades in America, electrifying the radical East Side after months of mounting unrest in Russia.

citation.quote: The news of the Russian revolution of October 1905 was electrifying and carried us to ecstatic heights.

title: Mother Earth name conceived on a buggy ride
summary: While visiting the little farm one Sunday in early February, Goldman and Max Baginski went for a buggy ride during which she conceived the title Mother Earth for their new magazine.

citation.quote: While visiting the little farm one Sunday, Max and I went for a buggy ride. It was early in February, but already the air was perfumed by the balm of spring.

title: Death of Johann Most
summary: While Goldman was in Buffalo on tour for Mother Earth, news arrived that Johann Most had died in Cincinnati while on a lecture tour, fighting for his ideal to the very last.

citation.quote: While still in Buffalo, we received the news of the death of Johann Most. He had been on a lecture tour and had died in Cincinnati, fighting for his ideal to the very last.

title: First issue of Mother Earth published
summary: Goldman and Max Baginski launched their magazine Mother Earth, a sixty-four-page publication combining social ideas with new strivings in American art and letters.

citation.quote: It appeared on the first of March 1906, in sixty-four pages. Its name was *Mother Earth.*

title: Awaiting Sasha's release from prison
summary: As May 1906 arrived, Emma Goldman anxiously prepared for Alexander Berkman's release after fourteen years in prison, planning to meet him in Detroit at his request.

citation.quote: [ ... ] May 1906 came at last. Only two more weeks remained till Sasha's resurrection. I had become restless, assailed by perturbing thoughts.

title: Alexander Berkman released from prison
summary: After fourteen years of imprisonment for his attentat against Henry Clay Frick, Alexander Berkman was freed and reunited with Emma Goldman in Detroit at the home of Carl Nold.

citation.quote: Buffalo, Toronto, Montreal, meetings, crowds—I went through them in a daze, conscious only of one thought—the 18th of May, the date of Sasha's release. I reached Detroit on the early morning of that day, with the vision of Sasha impatiently pacing his cell before his final liberation.

title: Mother Earth Czolgosz memorial issue published
summary: Despite opposition from some comrades who threatened to withdraw support, Goldman dedicated the October 1906 issue of Mother Earth to Leon Czolgosz on the fifth anniversary of his death.

citation.quote: That number was to contain articles on Leon Czolgosz, in memory of the fifth anniversary of his death. Sasha and Max strongly favoured the idea of a memorial issue, but other comrades fought against it on the ground that anything about Czolgosz would hurt the cause as well as the magazine.

title: Berkman begins lecture tour after release
summary: Following publication of the Czolgosz memorial issue of Mother Earth, Berkman embarked on a lecture tour with stops in Albany, Syracuse, and Pittsburgh, despite the risk of re-arrest in Pennsylvania.

citation.quote: As soon as the magazine was off the press, Sasha began his tour. His first stops were Albany, Syracuse, and Pittsburgh.

title: Berkman disappears in Cleveland
summary: After his lecture in Cleveland, Berkman vanished, prompting a three-day search of police stations, hospitals, and morgues, with newspapers headlining the disappearance of the recently freed anarchist.

citation.quote: His next stop was Cleveland. On the day after his first meeting in that city I received a wire informing me that Sasha had left the house of the comrade with whom he had spent the night and had not yet returned.

title: Kropotkin readmitted to France
summary: While Goldman was still in Holland for the Amsterdam congress, news arrived that Peter Kropotkin had at last been readmitted to France after years of exile following his imprisonment and expulsion.

citation.quote: While we were yet in Holland, news had come that Peter Kropotkin had at last been readmitted to France.

title: Financial depression grips the country
summary: Through the winter of 1907 and 1908, the United States was in the grip of financial depression, with thousands of workers idle and in poverty in every large city while authorities suppressed discussion of the crisis.

citation.quote: All through the winter of 1907 and 1908 the country was in the grip of financial depression. Thousands of workers in every large city were idle, in poverty and misery.

title: Goldman meets Schapiro at Amsterdam anarchist conference
summary: EG met English anarchist and trade organizer Alexander Schapiro at an international anarchist conference in Amsterdam.

citation.quote: EG met English anarchist and trade organizer Alexander Schapiro (?-1946) in 1907 at an international anarchist conference in Amsterdam (see LML, 1970, 403).

title: Goldman sails to Europe for Amsterdam anarchist congress
summary: Emma Goldman and Max departed New York from the Holland-America pier in mid-August 1907, bound for the international anarchist congress in Amsterdam.

citation.quote: In the middle of August 1907 Max and I waved our friends good-bye from the Holland-America pier.

title: International Anarchist Congress meets in Amsterdam
summary: Eighty men and women from many countries gathered openly in monarchical Holland to discuss revolution, syndicalism, mass insurrection, and individual acts of violence, without interference from authorities.

citation.quote: Eighty men and women, most of them hounded and persecuted in their own countries, were here able to address large meetings, gather in daily session, and discuss openly such vital problems as revolution, syndicalism, mass insurrection, and individual acts of violence, without any interference from the authorities.

title: Free-speech fight in Chicago
summary: Goldman recalls the free-speech fight in Chicago in 1908, after which she had been unable to return to the city until this tour.

citation.quote: For the first time since the free-speech fight in Chicago in 1908 I could go back to that city.

title: Lazarus Overbuch attempts to kill Chicago police chief
summary: Lazarus Overbuch, a recent Russian immigrant, attempted to take the life of the Chicago police chief. The national press claimed the attempt was linked to a widespread anarchist conspiracy; Goldman denied knowing Overbuch.

citation.quote: In 1908 Lazarus Overbuch, a recent Russian immigrant, attempted to take the life of the Chicago police chief. The national press claimed the attempt was linked to a widespread anarchist conspiracy.

title: Goldman speaks at Workmen's Hall social, dragged from platform
summary: At a clandestine social and concert at the Workmen's Hall in Chicago, Goldman slipped past police, began to address the audience, and was pulled from the platform by the captain in charge. Ben Reitman was dragged out by officers.

citation.quote: On the evening of our social gathering, March 17, I succeeded in slipping away through the back entrance of Yampolsky's house while the detectives were waiting for me out in front. I got safely through the police lines near the hall.

title: New York vice crusade against white-slave traffic
summary: New York City reformers launched a vice crusade focused on the white-slave traffic, prompting Goldman to prepare a lecture on its causes and effects.

citation.quote: In the latter part of 1909 New York again experienced a vice crusade. The reformers had discovered the white-slave traffic!

title: Jack London purchases land in Sonoma County
summary: American novelist Jack London purchased a large tract of land near Glen Ellen in Sonoma County, California.

citation.quote: Jack London (1876-1916): American novelist and short-story writer. He often wrote about the individual in a struggle for survival against the powers of nature. In 1910, London purchased a large tract of land near Glen Ellen in Sonoma County, California.

title: Bombing of the Los Angeles Times Building
summary: The Los Angeles Times Building was bombed; David Caplan and Matthew Schmidt would later be tried in 1915 for their participation.

citation.quote: the fight for Caplan and Schmidt: David Caplan and Matthew Schmidt were tried in 1915 for participation in the 1910 bombing of the Los Angeles Times Building.

title: Goldman's white-slave traffic lecture published in Mother Earth
summary: Goldman's lecture on the white-slave traffic was published in the January issue of Mother Earth and subsequently in pamphlet form.

citation.quote: The lecture was published in the January issue of Mother Earth and subsequently in pamphlet form.

title: Mother Earth's January issue held up by Comstock
summary: Copies of the January Mother Earth were held up by postal authorities on Anthony Comstock's complaint over Goldman's white-slave traffic article; Berkman secured its release after extended pressure.

citation.quote: He was informed that some copies had been held up on the complaint of Anthony Comstock. While we felt flattered that we were at last given a place among other victims of Comstockery, we nevertheless demanded to know the reason for the unexpected honour.

title: Berkman decides to write his prison memoirs
summary: On the anniversary of Alexander Berkman's release from prison, a telegram from him reached Goldman in Los Angeles announcing his decision to begin writing his prison memoirs.

citation.quote: May 18, the day of Sasha's resurrection, remained graven on my heart, although my yearly tours had always prevented my being with him on the anniversary of his release. ... On May 18 this year a telegram from him found me in Los Angeles. It filled me with great joy, for it brought the news that he had determined to begin his prison memoirs.

title: Berkman completes Prison Memoirs at Hudson retreat
summary: During the summer at their retreat on the Hudson, Berkman resumed work on his book and by the end of the summer had completed his Prison Memoirs, which Goldman hailed as a brilliant study of criminal psychology.

citation.quote: During the summer Sasha and I again went out to our retreat on the Hudson and he resumed work on his book. ... The end of the summer saw his *Prison Memoirs* completed.

title: Goldman and Reitman begin annual lecture tour; Anarchism and Other Essays published
summary: Goldman and Ben Reitman set out on their annual tour, just as her first book, Anarchism and Other Essays, came off the press, containing a biographic sketch by Hippolyte Havel.

citation.quote: In January 1911 Ben and I again started on our annual tour. Before we left, my selected lectures, *Anarchism and Other Essays,* came off the press.

title: Publication of Berkman's Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist
summary: Alexander Berkman's Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist appeared, widely reviewed and acclaimed as a moving human document comparing him to Slavic realists like Dostoyevsky.

citation.quote: The year 1912, rich with varied experiences, closed with three important events: the appearance of Sasha's book, the twenty-fifth anniversary of the eleventh of November, and the seventieth birthday of Peter Kropotkin.

title: Woodrow Wilson nominated for presidency
summary: Woodrow Wilson was nominated for the presidency and advocated neutrality for America in World War I until 1917.

citation.quote: Nominated for the presidency in 1912, Woodrow Wilson advocated neutrality for America in World War I until 1917, when he asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany.

title: Ben Reitman's night ride and torture in San Diego
summary: Ben Reitman was abducted by fourteen Vigilantes in San Diego and subjected to beatings and humiliation on this date.

citation.quote: the night ride in 1912 had on Ben

title: Twenty-fifth anniversary of the Haymarket martyrs
summary: Goldman spoke at the twenty-fifth anniversary commemoration of the November 11, 1887 execution of the Chicago Haymarket martyrs, paying tribute to the men whose deaths had become a decisive influence in her life.

citation.quote: November II, 1887—November 11, 1912! Twenty-five years, an infinitesimal fraction of time in the upward march of the race, but an eternity for him who dies many deaths in the course of his life.

title: Suppressed lecture experience in San Diego
summary: Goldman recalls her experience in San Diego two years prior to 1915, when her lecture was suppressed by Vigilantes.

citation.quote: Our experience in San Diego two years previously, in 1913, had exerted the same effect on me as the night ride in 1912 had on Ben.

title: D. H. Lawrence publishes Sons and Lovers
summary: D. H. Lawrence's partly autobiographical novel Sons and Lovers was published, describing an enduring emotionally wrought bond between the central character Paul Morel and his protective mother.

citation.quote: Sons and Lovers by D. H. Lawrence: Published in 1913, Lawrence's partly autobiographical novel describes an enduring and emotionally wrought bond between the central character, Paul Morel, and his devoted and protective mother.

title: Helen Keller publishes Out of the Dark
summary: Helen Keller, a member of the Socialist Party of Massachusetts, published "Out of the Dark," a series of essays on socialism.

citation.quote: After obtaining a bachelor of arts degree from Radcliffe College, she became a member of the Socialist Party of Massachusetts, publishing "Out of the Dark" in 1913, a series of essays on socialism.

title: Failed attempt to secure a San Diego hall
summary: In 1914 one of Goldman's friends went to San Diego to try to secure a hall for her lecture, but socialists and other radical groups refused, forcing the plan to be abandoned temporarily.

citation.quote: In 1914 one of our friends had gone to San Diego to try to secure a hall. The socialists, who had their own place, refused to have anything to do with me.

title: Founding of the 'Save the Children' organization
summary: The 'Save the Children' society, dedicated to aiding destitute Russian children, was founded in 1914 and continued its work through the war and revolution despite repeated Bolshevik raids.

citation.quote: The other was the head of the 'Save the Children' organization, founded in 1914 and continued through all the vicissitudes of the intervening years.

title: Wilson's New Freedom program enacted
summary: Woodrow Wilson's New Freedom economic reform program, named in his 1912 presidential campaign speeches, was enacted in a series of congressional acts.

citation.quote: The New Freedom: economic reform program named in Woodrow Wilson's 1912 presidential campaign speeches. It was enacted in a series of congressional acts in 1914.

title: Goldman publishes The Social Significance of the Modern Drama
summary: Goldman's book The Social Significance of the Modern Drama was published.

citation.quote: The Social Significance of the Modern Drama was published in April 1914.

title: Ludlow massacre
summary: The National Guard opened fire on a tent city of coal-mine strikers in Ludlow, Colorado. The resulting deaths, including women and children, precipitated widespread sympathy for the miners and armed resistance.

citation.quote: the Ludlow massacres: one of America's bloodiest assaults on organized labor. On April 20, 1914, the National Guard opened fire on a tent city of coal-mine strikers in Ludlow, Colorado.

title: Outbreak of war in Europe
summary: Goldman notes that three months had passed since the outbreak of war in Europe as she prepared her drama course and lectures on the war, placing the outbreak about three months before her November 10, 1914 lecture.

citation.quote: I was busy preparing the new drama course I had promised to deliver in Chicago and a series of lectures on the war. Three months had passed since its outbreak in Europe.

title: Germany invades Belgium
summary: The German army invaded Belgium, terrorizing the population, looting and burning towns.

citation.quote: what the Germans had done to the Belgians: In August 1914 the German army invaded Belgium, terrorizing the population, looting and burning towns.

title: Goldman's drama lecture on Haymarket anniversary in Chicago
summary: Goldman opened her first Chicago drama talk by contrasting the public attitude toward anarchism between 1887 and 1914, invoking the Haymarket martyrs on the eve of the anniversary of their execution; her wealthy patrons and some attendees were shocked and walked out.

citation.quote: My first drama talk fell on November 10, a day of momentous importance to me. It had been the last day on earth of my comrades martyred in Chicago twenty-seven years before. I introduced my lecture by contrasting the changes in the public attitude towards anarchism between 1887 and 1914.

title: Trial of Caplan and Schmidt
summary: David Caplan and Matthew Schmidt were tried for participation in the 1910 bombing of the Los Angeles Times Building.

citation.quote: the fight for Caplan and Schmidt: David Caplan and Matthew Schmidt were tried in 1915 for participation in the 1910 bombing of the Los Angeles Times Building.

title: Goldman's return to San Diego
summary: Goldman returned to San Diego accompanied by Sasha (Berkman), Fitzi, Ben Capes, and Leon Bass to deliver her suppressed lecture, and held a meeting on Ibsen's Enemy of the People despite Vigilante presence.

citation.quote: May 14, 1912—June 20, 1915—what an incredible change! Yet what might be awaiting us in San Diego?

title: Warren K. Billings convicted and sentenced to life
summary: Sasha telegraphed Goldman that Billings had been convicted and sentenced to prison for life in connection with the Preparedness Parade bombing, prompting her to leave Provincetown for New York.

citation.quote: Then came Sasha’s telegram informing me that Billings had been convicted and sentenced to prison for life. There was no more hesitancy on my part. I prepared to leave for New York.

title: Raid on Margaret Sanger's Brooklyn clinic
summary: Margaret Sanger, her sister Ethel Byrne, and assistant Fanya Mandell were arrested in a raid on Sanger's birth-control clinic in Brooklyn.

citation.quote: Margaret Sanger, her sister Ethel Byrne, a trained nurse, and their assistant, Fanya Mandell, were rounded up in a raid on Mrs. Sanger’s clinic in Brooklyn.

title: Reitman arrested in Cleveland for birth-control pamphlets
summary: At Goldman's Cleveland lecture on "Family Limitation," Ben Reitman called for volunteers to distribute birth-control pamphlets and was arrested. A hundred supporters followed him to the jail.

citation.quote: At my lecture in Cleveland on “Family Limitation” Ben conceived the idea of calling for volunteers to distribute birth-control pamphlets. A number of people responded. At the end of the meeting Ben was arrested.

title: Reitman convicted in Cleveland birth-control case
summary: Ben Reitman was found guilty in Cleveland and sentenced to six months in the workhouse and a thousand-dollar fine, the heaviest penalty imposed for a birth-control offence.

citation.quote: Ben was found guilty and sentenced to six months in the workhouse and to pay a thousand dollars’ fine. It was the heaviest penalty imposed for a birth-control offence.

title: Mooney convicted and sentenced to death
summary: Tom Mooney was convicted and sentenced to death for the Preparedness Parade bombing. Goldman attributes the verdict to the open-shop bosses seeking to crush labor organizing.

citation.quote: Tom Mooney had been convicted and sentenced to death. ... The bosses who had declared themselves for the “open shop” had determined to hang Tom Mooney, as a warning to other labour organizers, and Mooney’s doom was sealed.

title: Everett IWW case
summary: In Everett, Washington, seventy-four I.W.W. members were on trial fighting for their lives, while jails across the country held men convicted for their ideals.

citation.quote: In Everett, Washington, seventy-four I.W.W. boys were fighting for their lives, and in every other State of the Union the jails and prisons were filled with men convicted for their ideals.

title: Mooney and Billings imprisoned in California
summary: Thomas J. Mooney, leader of the left wing of the California Federation of Labor, and Warren Billings were convicted and would serve 23 years in California prisons, in spite of evidence that testimony against them was perjured.

citation.quote: Thomas J. Mooney, leader of the left wing of the California Federation of Labor, and Warren Billings were convicted and would serve 23 years (1916-39) in California prisons, in spite of evidence that testimony against them was perjured.

title: Joyce publishes A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
summary: James Joyce's partly autobiographical novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, describing a sensitive youth harried by religious and sexual guilt, was published.

citation.quote: A Portrait of the Artist As a Young Man: Partly autobiographical, James Joyce's Portrait, published in 1916, describes a sensitive youth, harried by religious and sexual guilt.

title: Brandeis serves on the U.S. Supreme Court
summary: Louis D. Brandeis served as an Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.

citation.quote: Louis D. Brandeis (1856-1941): U.S. Supreme Court justice, 1916-1939.

title: Easter Uprising in Dublin
summary: About 1,250 Irish rebels attempted to capture the most prominent buildings in Dublin to challenge British rule.

citation.quote: "Easter uprising": On Easter Monday in 1916 about 1,250 Irish rebels attempted to capture the most prominent buildings in Dublin to challenge British rule.

title: Arrest of Mooney, Billings and others after bombing
summary: Following the Preparedness Parade explosion, four labor men and one woman were arrested: Thomas J. Mooney and his wife Rena, Warren K. Billings, Edward D. Nolan, and Israel Weinberg.
