citation.quote: A reign of official terror followed the explosion. Revolutionary workers and anarchists were, as always, the first victims. Four labour men and one woman were immediately arrested. They were Thomas J. Mooney and his wife, Rena, Warren K. Billings, Edward D. Nolan, and Israel Weinberg.

title: Anti-preparedness mass meeting in San Francisco
summary: Liberal and progressive labor elements held an anti-preparedness mass meeting in San Francisco, the same evening Goldman's lecture on "Preparedness" had originally been scheduled.

citation.quote: My lecture on “Preparedness” had originally been scheduled for the 20th. But we learned that the liberal and progressive labour elements had arranged an anti-preparedness mass meeting for the same evening, and, not wishing to conflict with the occasion, postponed my talk for the 22nd.

title: Preparedness Parade bombing in San Francisco
summary: A bomb exploded during the Preparedness Parade in San Francisco, killing and wounding marchers. Newspapers immediately blamed anarchists.

citation.quote: On Saturday, July 22, 1916, I was lunching with them. It was a golden California day, and the three of us were in a bright mood.

title: Goldman delivers Preparedness lecture amid bomb panic
summary: On the evening following the explosion, only about fifty people attended Goldman's postponed lecture in San Francisco, with the rest of the audience consisting of detectives.

citation.quote: On the evening following the explosion there were just fifty people at my meeting, the rest of the audience consisting of detectives.

title: Russian Revolution brings hope
summary: Goldman writes that after a darkening political sky in the United States, hope arrived from Russia: the long-yearned-for Revolution had come.

citation.quote: Then, unexpectedly, the light of hope broke in the east. It came from Russia, the land tsar-ridden for centuries. The day so long yearned for had arrived at last—the Revolution had come!

title: Goldman transported to Jefferson City penitentiary
summary: [Inference] After conviction under the Espionage Law, Goldman was escorted by deputy marshals on a train to the Missouri State Penitentiary at Jefferson City to begin her sentence.

citation.quote: Arriving in Jefferson City, my escorts offered to take me to the penitentiary in a taxi. I requested that we walk. It might be my last chance for a long while, I thought.

title: Brandeis signs appeal application; Goldman released on bail
summary: Two weeks after her delivery to the prison, Harry Weinberger secured Supreme Court Justice Louis D. Brandeis's signature on the appeal application, admitting Goldman and Berkman to bail and temporary freedom.

citation.quote: Two weeks after I had been delivered to the prison, the same deputy marshal and his wife arrived to take me back to New York. Irrepressible Harry Weinberger had succeeded in getting Supreme Court Justice Louis D. Brandeis to sign the application for our appeal, which admitted Sasha and me to bail and temporary freedom.

title: Berkman indicted for murder in the Mooney case
summary: Goldman learned that Berkman had been indicted for murder in connection with the Mooney case in San Francisco, after the Chamber of Commerce and District Attorney sought revenge for his exposure of the frame-up against Mooney and Billings.

citation.quote: Her tone and manner filled me with apprehension. Urged to tell me the worst, she informed me that Sasha was wanted in San Francisco. He had been indicted for murder in connexion with the Mooney case.

title: Russian refugees depart with message to soviets
summary: Russian refugees departed in May and June carrying a message from Goldman and her comrades to the councils of workers, soldiers, and sailors in Russia regarding the San Francisco cases and Berkman.

citation.quote: It was the answer to the message we had sent to the councils of workers, soldiers, and sailors by the refugees that had departed in May and June.

title: Petrograd and Kronstadt demonstrations for Berkman and Mooney
summary: Demonstrations took place in Petrograd and Kronstadt in support of Berkman and the San Francisco defendants, in response to messages sent by Russian refugees returning home after the revolution.

citation.quote: Our activities for Sasha and the San Francisco cases received unexpected and far-reaching impetus through news from Russia : demonstrations in their behalf had taken place in Petrograd and Kronstadt.

title: Kronstadt sailors demand hostage Ambassador Francis
summary: A resolution from the Kronstadt sailors called for the arrest of American Ambassador Francis as hostage until the San Francisco victims and Berkman were freed; armed sailors marched to the American Embassy in Petrograd.

citation.quote: A resolution proposed by the sailors of Kronstadt and adopted at a monster meeting called for the arrest of Mr. Francis, the American Ambassador in Russia, who was to be held as hostage until the San Francisco victims and Sasha should be free. A delegation of armed sailors had marched to the American Embassy in Petrograd to carry out the decision.

title: Berkman extradition to California postponed
summary: After labor delegation pressure on Governor Whitman, District Attorney Fickert wired Albany that 'the Berkman extradition would not be pressed for the present,' temporarily averting Berkman's transfer to San Francisco.

citation.quote: It was a victory indeed, though it did only temporarily delay proceedings. But instead of sending the requested documents, the San Francisco prosecutor wired Albany that "the Berkman extradition would not be pressed for the present."

title: Tulsa IWW members tarred and feathered
summary: Seventeen I.W.W. comrades were tarred and feathered in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and left half-dead in the sage-brush during the wartime repression of radicals.

citation.quote: In Tulsa, Oklahoma, seventeen of their comrades were tarred and feathered and in a half-dead condition left in the sage-brush.

title: Mass arrest of IWW members in Chicago
summary: One hundred and sixty I.W.W. members were arrested in Chicago and held for trial on charges of treason during the wartime suppression of radical organizations.

citation.quote: One hundred and sixty I.W.W.'s were arrested in Chicago and held for trial on charges of treason.

title: Mother Earth suppressed under Espionage Law
summary: Mother Earth became the first publication suppressed under the new Espionage Law, soon followed by the Blast, the Masses, and other radical periodicals, with indictments brought against their editorial staffs.

citation.quote: Even private distribution had become impossible for any paper opposed to the war. Mother Earth became the first victim, soon followed by the Blast, the Masses, and other publications, and by indictments against their editorial staffs.

title: Wilson asks Congress to declare war on Germany
summary: President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany, ending years of advocating American neutrality in World War I.

citation.quote: Nominated for the presidency in 1912, Woodrow Wilson advocated neutrality for America in World War I until 1917, when he asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany.

title: Immigration Act of 1917 enacted
summary: The Immigration Act of 1917 made any alien political radical deportable, no matter how nonviolent his speech or practice.

citation.quote: Federal deportation mania: The Immigration Act of 1917 made any alien political radical deportable, no matter how nonviolent his speech or practice.

title: Establishment of the Cheka
summary: The All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage (Vehcheka), a Soviet police organization, was established to carry out investigative functions; through its local branches it gained powers including summary trials and executions.

citation.quote: The All-Russian Extraordinary Commisson for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage (the Veh Cheka) was a Soviet police organization intended after its establishment in 1917 to carry out investigative functions.

title: Lunacharsky serves as commissar of education
summary: Anatol Lunacharsky served as commissar of education in the Soviet government, directing the development of new socialist education and culture.

citation.quote: Anatol Lunacharsky (1875-1933): As commissar of education in the Soviet government, 1917-29, he directed the development of new socialist education and culture.

title: Goldman acquitted of birth-control charge in New York
summary: Denied a jury trial, Goldman's case came up before three judges. The detectives' contradictory evidence about her distributing birth-control pamphlets on Union Square in May collapsed and she was acquitted.

citation.quote: On January 8 my case came up before three judges. Presiding Judge Cullen warned me severely that he would not permit any theories of the defendant to be aired in court. ... I was acquitted.

title: February Revolution overthrows Czarist government
summary: The czarist government was overthrown and replaced by a provisional government in the first of two 1917 Russian revolutions.

citation.quote: The October Revolution: In 1917 Russia underwent two revolutions. In February the czarist government was overthrown and replaced by a provisional government.

title: Twelfth anniversary of Berkman's release from prison
summary: May 18 marked the twelfth anniversary of Sasha Berkman's release from the Western Penitentiary of Pennsylvania, the first time he and Goldman were together on the same platform in years.

citation.quote: We felt that May 18 was the beginning of a period of historic importance. To Sasha and myself the day had also a profound personal meaning. It was the twelfth anniversary of his resurrection from the Western Penitentiary of Pennsylvania, the first time in years that he and I were together in the same city and on the same platform.

title: Mother Earth issues black-draped June issue
summary: The June issue of Mother Earth appeared draped in black, its cover depicting a tomb inscribed 'IN MEMORIAM—AMERICAN DEMOCRACY,' protesting conscription.

citation.quote: The June issue of Mother Earth appeared draped in black, its cover representing a tomb bearing the inscription: "IN MEMORIAM—AMERICAN DEMOCRACY."

title: Espionage Act enacted
summary: The new Espionage Law was enacted, making interference with the military or obstruction of the draft illegal.

citation.quote: The new Espionage Law: Enacted in June 1917, the law made interference with the military or obstruction of the draft illegal.

title: Conscription bill becomes law; registration day set
summary: The U.S. conscription bill became law, with registration day set for June 4. Goldman saw it as the death of American democracy.

citation.quote: Returning from the meeting home we heard news-boys shouting extra night editions—the conscription bill had become a law! Registration day was set for June 4. The thought struck me that on that day American democracy would be carried to its grave.

title: No-Conscription mass meeting at Hunt's Point Palace
summary: Goldman and Berkman held a No-Conscription mass meeting at Hunt's Point Palace in New York with tens of thousands attending. Goldman closed the meeting to prevent bloodshed as soldiers and police threatened violence.

citation.quote: Incidentally the papers also gave wide publicity to our meeting scheduled for June 4. [ . . . ] When we got within half a dozen blocks of Hunt's Point Palace, our taxi had to come to a stop.

title: Forward Hall anti-conscription meeting
summary: Goldman held an anti-conscription meeting at Forward Hall on June 14. After receiving a phone warning of a plot to kill her, the meeting proceeded; afterward federal officers detained men without registration cards.

citation.quote: We scheduled a mass meeting for June 14. It was not necessary for us to print announcements. We merely called up the newspapers, and they did the rest.

title: Arrest of Goldman and Berkman by U.S. Marshal
summary: United States Marshal Thomas D. McCarthy arrested Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman at their offices the day after the Forward Hall meeting, charging them with conspiracy against the draft.

citation.quote: On the following afternoon we were all busy in our offices. Sasha and Fitzi were on the upper floor, preparing the next issue of the Blast. [ . . . ] Above the hum of conversation and the clicking of the typewriter we suddenly heard the heavy stamping of feet on the stairway, and before any one of us had a chance to see what was the matter, a dozen men burst into my office. The leader of the party excitedly cried: "Emma Goldman, you're under arrest! And so is Berkman; where is he?"

title: Berkman released from the Tombs on bail
summary: After raising a $25,000 cash bond, Alexander Berkman was released from the Tombs prison on June 25, 1917.

citation.quote: At last we succeeded in procuring the twenty-five-thousand-dollar cash bond demanded for Sasha, and on June 25 he was released from the Tombs.

title: Trial of Goldman and Berkman begins
summary: On June 27, 1917, Goldman's 48th birthday, she and Berkman appeared in the Federal Building courtroom to face the conspiracy-against-the-draft prosecution.

citation.quote: It was Tuesday, June 27, at 10 a.m., when, together with Sasha, still on crutches, I walked through the crowded court-room in the Federal Building to face the prosecution.

title: Bisbee deportation of IWW workers
summary: Twelve hundred I.W.W. members were manhandled and driven across the border at Bisbee, Arizona, amid the wartime patriotic crackdown that followed America's entry into the war.

citation.quote: In Bisbee, Arizona, twelve hundred I.W.W.'s were manhandled and driven across the border. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, seventeen of their comrades were tarred and feathered and in a half-dead condition left in the sage-brush.

title: Closing arguments in Goldman–Berkman trial
summary: The final round of the trial — closing arguments by the prosecutor, Berkman, and Goldman — was set for July 9, 1917. The jury convicted them after 39 minutes of deliberation.

citation.quote: After endlessly repetitious "evidence" of our crime, which in reality proved nothing, the prosecution closed its case. The last round in the contest between ideas and organized stupidity was set for July 9.

title: Kerensky becomes prime minister of provisional government
summary: Alexander Kerensky became prime minister of the Russian provisional government, serving until October 1917 when he fled St. Petersburg.

citation.quote: Alexander Kerensky (1881-1970): prime minister of the provisional government from July 21, 1917, to October 1917; he fled St. Petersburg.

title: October Revolution in Russia
summary: The October Revolution overthrew the Kerensky government and brought the Bolsheviks to power, fulfilling promises that the February Revolution had only begun.

citation.quote: The October Revolution suddenly rent the clouds, its flames spreading to the remotest corners of the earth, carrying the message of fulfilment of the supreme promise the February Revolution had held out.

title: October Revolution
summary: The Bolshevik party led Russian workers and peasants to overthrow the provisional government.

citation.quote: In October the Bolshevik party led Russian workers and peasants to overthrow the provisional government.

title: New Year's party at Stella and Teddy's
summary: Goldman saw out the intensely active year of 1917 with a New Year's party at Stella and Teddy's quarters, pausing briefly from political struggle.

citation.quote: 1917 had been a year of most intense activity, and it deserved to receive a fitting farewell. Our New Year's party in Stella's and Teddy's quarters appropriately performed the pagan rites.

title: Espionage Act renamed Sedition Act
summary: The Espionage Law was renamed the Sedition Act in 1918, its punishments stiffened, and "disloyal" language about the government prohibited.

citation.quote: Renamed the Sedition Act in 1918, its punishments were stiffened, and "disloyal" language about the government was prohibited.

title: Russian Civil War
summary: Russian civil war fought between Bolsheviks and counterrevolutionary military leaders Anton Denikin, Alexander Kolchak, and Nikolai Yudenich.

citation.quote: Anton Denikin (1872-1947), Alexander Kolchak (1873-1920), and Nikolai Yudenich (1862-1933): military leaders in the counterrevolution against the Bolsheviks during the civil war (1918-20).

title: Supreme Court declines Goldman rehearing
summary: The United States Supreme Court declined to grant Goldman and Berkman a rehearing or further delay, setting February 5 as the date for their recommitment to prison.

citation.quote: The end of January terminated the hopes many of our friends had naively entertained. The Supreme Court declined to grant us a rehearing or to delay the course of legal justice further. February 5 was set for our recommitment to prison.

title: Goldman surrenders to begin prison sentence
summary: After bidding farewell to friends in the early hours of February 4, Goldman surrendered at the Federal Building and was taken to the Jefferson City penitentiary by deputy marshal.

citation.quote: It was late, or rather early February 4, when our friends bade us hail and farewell. There were still the proofs to be read of my brochure The Truth about the Bolsheviki, but Fitzi considerately undertook to see the pamphlet safely through.

title: Goldman's birthday in Jefferson City prison
summary: Goldman's fellow coloured prisoners prepared a full task of jackets in advance so she could remain out of the shop on her birthday, and she received letters, telegrams, flowers, and packages from comrades.

citation.quote: On the eve of June 27 my coloured friends presented me with a full task of jackets for the following day. They had remembered my birthday.

title: Death of David in the Argonne forest
summary: Goldman's nephew David was killed in the Bois de Rappe in the Argonne forest, one month before Armistice Day, after refusing the safety of a military orchestra assignment.

citation.quote: He lost his life on October 15, 1918, in the Bois de Rappe, in the Argonne forest, killed one month before Armistice Day, in the prime and glory of his youth.

title: Armistice Day observed in Missouri penitentiary
summary: Work was halted in the prison shop on Armistice Day; inmates were given a holiday as the declaration of armistice ending the war was celebrated.

citation.quote: On November 11, at ten in the morning, the electric power in our shop was switched off, the machines stopped, and we were informed that there would be no further work that day.

title: Denikin's pogrom in Fastov
summary: In 1919 the White general Denikin's forces conducted a week-long pogrom in Fastov, Ukraine, killing four thousand Jews outright and thousands more in flight to Kiev, with widespread rape and the destruction of much of the town.

citation.quote: But the pogrom organized in 1919 by Denikin had been the most fiendish one. It had lasted a whole week and had taken the lives of four thousand persons outright and of several thousand more that had perished while escaping to Kiev.

title: Palmer Raids against political radicals
summary: As U.S. attorney general, Mitchell Palmer mounted an attack against political radicals in the United States, rounding up anarchists and Communists and arresting thousands of immigrant aliens whose political work was mostly social and educational.

citation.quote: Mitchell Palmer (1872-1936): U.S. attorney general and congress-man. As attorney general in 1919, Palmer mounted an attack against political radicals in the United States, rounding up anarchists and Communists, arresting thousands of immigrant aliens...

title: Kalinin formal head of Soviet state
summary: Mikhail Kalinin served as the formal head of the Soviet state.

citation.quote: Mikhail Kalinin (1875-1946): formal head of the Soviet state 1919-46.

title: Lansbury edits the Daily Herald
summary: British Labour Party politician George Lansbury, founder of the Daily Herald, served as its editor.

citation.quote: George Lansbury (1859-1940): journalist, British Labour Party politician, and socialist historian. The founder of the Daily Herald, he was editor during 1919-1923.

title: John Reed publishes Ten Days That Shook the World
summary: Journalist and political radical John Reed achieved international prominence with Ten Days That Shook the World, considered the best reporting of the Bolshevik revolution.

citation.quote: An eyewitness observer of the events in Russia, John Reed achieved international prominence with his Ten Days That Shook the World (1919), considered the best reporting of the Bolshevik revolution.

title: Murder of Liebknecht, Luxemburg, and Landauer
summary: Karl Liebknecht (German socialist anti-militarist), Rosa Luxemburg (Polish-born socialist revolutionary), and Gustav Landauer (German anarchist) were murdered by antirevolutionary soldiers in Germany.

citation.quote: Karl Liebnecht (1871-1919): German socialist and active anti-militarist, murdered by German soldiers in 1919. Rosa Luxemburg (1871-1919): Polish-born socialist, revolutionary... murdered by antirevolutionary soldiers in Germany in 1919. Gustav Landauer (1870-1919) German anarchist murdered by antirevolutionary soldiers in Germany in 1919.

title: Balabanoff elected secretary at First International Congress
summary: Russian politician Angelica Balabanoff was elected secretary at the First International Congress.

citation.quote: Angelica Balabanoff (1877-1965): Russian politician, active in Russian and Italian socialist movements. Elected secretary at the First International Congress in 1919, she emigrated from Russia in 1924 as an anti-Bolshevik.

title: Berkman held in solitary at Atlanta for seven and a half months
summary: After being punished in 'the tomb' for interceding for a Black prisoner, Berkman was held continuously in solitary and isolation from February 21 to October 1, 1919, the day of his discharge.

citation.quote: After that he remained continuously in solitary and isolation for seven-and-a-half months, from February 21 to the day of his discharge, October 1.

title: Third International convened in Moscow
summary: The Third International was convened in Moscow to implement the dictatorship of the proletariat.

citation.quote: The Third International was convened in Moscow in March 1919 to implement the dictatorship of the proletariat.

title: Kate Richards O'Hare arrives at Missouri penitentiary
summary: Kate Richards O'Hare, convicted under the Espionage Law, joined Goldman as a political prisoner in the Missouri penitentiary, forming a 'trinity' with Goldman and Ella.

citation.quote: April added another political, Mrs. Kate Richards O'Hare, to our company. I had met her once before, when she had called at the prison on her visit to Jefferson City to see Governor Gardner.

title: Goldman's fiftieth birthday in Missouri penitentiary
summary: Goldman spent her fiftieth birthday imprisoned at the Missouri penitentiary, reflecting on thirty years in the firing line as she pedalled her sewing-machine.

citation.quote: Such thoughts and queries swirled through my brain as I pedalled my sewing-machine on June 27, 1919.

title: Goldman and Berkman complete twenty months of sentence
summary: Goldman and Berkman had completed twenty months of their two-year sentence, having earned four months each for good behaviour, but were required to serve an extra month for an unpaid $20,000 fine.

citation.quote: On August 28, 1919, Sasha and I had completed twenty months of our two-year sentence. Wicked anarchists though we were, we had earned four months each for good behaviour.

title: Goldman released from Missouri penitentiary
summary: Goldman left the Missouri penitentiary accompanied by her niece Stella, and after making an affidavit of poverty and a $15,000 bond was secured, she was at liberty pending an immigration inquiry.

citation.quote: Saturday, September 28, 1919, I left the Missouri penitentiary, accompanied by my faithful Stella, who had come from New York for the occasion.

title: Alexander Berkman released from Atlanta penitentiary
summary: Sasha (Alexander Berkman) was released from the Atlanta federal penitentiary three days late, on October 1 instead of September 28, after twenty-one months that left him a physical wreck.

citation.quote: Harry Weinberger had gone to Atlanta to meet Sasha on his release. The fates had never been kind to him in prison; this time they robbed him of three days. Instead of September 28, Sasha was released on October 1.

title: Goldman's deportation hearing
summary: Emma Goldman's deportation hearing, twice postponed, was finally set for October 27. She refused to answer questions and submitted a written protest against the Anti-Anarchist Law.

citation.quote: My deportation hearing, twice postponed, was finally set for October 27. Sasha had already made his statement prior to leaving Atlanta.

title: Death of Henry Clay Frick announced at Chicago farewell dinner
summary: During a farewell dinner in Chicago, reporters brought news of Henry Clay Frick's death. Berkman responded 'Deported by God,' and Goldman noted Frick would be remembered only through his connection to Berkman.

citation.quote: During the farewell dinner given us by our friends in Chicago, on December 2, reporters dashed in with the news of Henry Clay Frick's death.

title: Goldman and Berkman surrender for deportation at Ellis Island
summary: Following a Federal Department of Labor deportation order, Goldman and Berkman surrendered at Ellis Island on December 5, with Harry Weinberger seeking return of their thirty thousand dollar bond.

citation.quote: The next morning brought a telegram from Harry Weinberger informing us that the Federal Department of Labor had ordered our deportation, and that we must surrender on December 5.

title: Supreme Court denies writ of error in deportation case
summary: Harry Weinberger argued his motion before Chief Justice White, but the Court denied the writ of error and refused a stay of deportation for Alexander Berkman.

citation.quote: Harry successfully appealed to Chief Justice White. On December 11 he was permitted to argue his motion, but the Court denied us the writ of error. A stay of deportation for Sasha was also refused.

title: Final visiting day on Ellis Island before deportation
summary: A hectic Saturday on Ellis Island with visits from friends and reporters, as Goldman and Berkman awaited deportation. Authorities had assured them they would not be sent away before Christmas.

citation.quote: Saturday, December 20, was a hectic day, with vague indications that it might be our last. We had been assured by the Ellis Island authorities that we were not likely to be sent away before Christmas, certainly not for several days to come.

title: Deportation of Goldman and Berkman aboard the Buford
summary: At 4:20 A.M., Goldman, Berkman, and 247 other radicals were transported by barge from Ellis Island to the Buford, beginning their forced deportation to Soviet Russia.

citation.quote: I looked at my watch. It was 4:20 A.M. on the day of our Lord, December 21, 1919.

title: Goldman returns to Petrograd from Moscow
summary: Goldman returned to Petrograd, where she learned via letters from Stella Ballantine and Fitzi that her sister Helena had died, allegedly as a result of the shock of Goldman's deportation.

citation.quote: Mail was actually awaiting us there, received four weeks previously. Why had it not been forwarded, we asked Liza Zorin. 'What was the use?' she replied; 'I did not think anything from America so important and interesting as what you must have seen and heard in Moscow.' The letters were from Fitzi and Stella. Not 'so important'—only news of the death of my beloved Helena.

title: Ninth Party Congress militarizes labour
summary: The ninth Communist Party Congress imposed militarization of labour and one-man management of factories, replacing workers' control with appointed specialists. Goldman called it a destruction of October's principal achievements.

citation.quote: The militarization of labour, rushed through the ninth Party Congress with typical Tammany Hall steam-roller methods, definitely turned every worker into a galley-slave. The substitution of one-man power in the shops and mills in place of co-operative management placed the masses again under the thumb of the very elements they had for three years been taught to hate as the worst menace.

title: Bertrand Russell arrives with British Labour Mission
summary: The British Labour Mission, including Bertrand Russell, arrived in Petrograd. Most members were feted with elaborate ceremonies, while Russell politely refused official chaperones and rejected privileged quarters.

citation.quote: The mission at last arrived, most of its members of the usual Anglo-Saxon better-than-thou attitude. They were against intervention, of course, and they boasted of having repudiated the attacks on Soviet Russia, but as to revolution or communism, no, thank you, none of that for them.

title: Expedition visits prison in Kharkov
summary: Goldman and Berkman toured the Kharkov detention camp and prison, where they found an old peasant woman associated with Makhno held in solitary confinement and a man awaiting execution as a counter-revolutionary.

citation.quote: We decided to visit the local prison and detention camp. \[ ... \] Both penal institutions bore out the statement of our engineering acquaintance as regards Ukrainian Communist management and despotism.

title: Expedition reaches Poltava
summary: After Kharkov, the expedition stopped at Poltava, where the Revkom granted them carte blanche to Soviet departments. Goldman met the daughter of Vladimir Korolenko and the head of the 'Save the Children' society.

citation.quote: Our credentials from the centre found greater favour in Poltava than in Kharkov. The secretary of the Revkom (revolutionary committee acting as the local government) received us pleasantly and gave us carte blanche to every Soviet department.

title: Goldman and Alsberg visit Vladimir Korolenko
summary: Goldman and Henry Alsberg called on the writer Vladimir Korolenko at his Poltava home. The convalescing author condemned Bolshevik terror and hostage-taking as a travesty of revolutionary ethics.

citation.quote: In the morning, still in the throes of the preceding evening, I went, together with Henry Alsberg, to the Korolenko home. It was a little green gem, entirely hidden from view by trees and vines—an enchanting place, with its old native furniture, ornate copper, brass, and colourful Ukrainian peasant handiwork.

title: Expedition reaches devastated Fastov
summary: On the way to Kiev, the expedition was forced to stop at Fastov. Goldman and Berkman were received in the synagogue and heard the survivors' account of Denikin's 1919 pogrom that had nearly destroyed the town's Jewish community.

citation.quote: Our next destination was to be Kiev, but the contrariness of Russian engines compelled us to stop at Fastov. We did not regret the delay. We had heard and read of ghastly anti-Jewish pogroms, but we had never before come face to face with their ravages.

title: Expedition arrives in Kiev after Polish withdrawal
summary: After six days of difficult travel, the expedition reached Kiev shortly after the Polish occupation ended. Local Communists were hostile to Moscow's credentials, and Goldman found the alleged Polish destruction had been propaganda exaggeration.

citation.quote: Our need for a thorough scrub and a real night's rest was compelling. Not less so was our eager anticipation of the rich material, particularly counter-revolutionary data, to be found in Kiev. The city on the Dnieper had been the pivot of all the battles in the Ukraine between the Red and the White forces. Only recently the Poles had invaded Kiev.

title: Gallina Makhno secretly visits Goldman in Kiev
summary: Gallina, the wife of Nestor Makhno, secretly visited Goldman in Kiev with a message from her husband proposing a staged abduction of Goldman and Berkman so he could explain his anarchist position to them. Goldman declined.

citation.quote: I was pulled back to reality by the arrival of Sonya Avrutskaya, a very sympathetic local comrade. With her was a stranger, a young woman in peasant costume, who was introduced to me as Gallina, the wife of Nestor Makhno.

title: Henry Alsberg arrested at Zhmerinka
summary: American correspondent Henry Alsberg was arrested at Zhmerinka station by order of the All-Russian Cheka because he had signed a telegram to Lenin on behalf of Albert Boni and had left Moscow without Cheka permission.

citation.quote: On the way to Odessa we lost our good friend Henry Alsberg. Inadvertently he had caused his own arrest. Henry had joined the expedition without having secured the consent of the Moscow Cheka and he could have continued till the end of our journey without the eagle eye of the Soviet being able to discover his whereabouts.

title: Expedition arrives in Odessa under martial law
summary: The expedition reached Odessa to find the city in darkness after a fire had destroyed the telegraph office and electric station, declared the work of White incendiaries. Martial law was imposed amid rumors of a Polish advance on Kiev and Wrangel's northern push.

citation.quote: At last we reached the great city on the Black Sea, only to find that a devastating fire had laid the main telegraph office and the electric station in ashes the previous day, leaving the city in utter darkness. The holocaust was declared to be the work of White incendiaries, and the city was placed under martial law.

title: Rosh Hashana with the Landesman family in Odessa
summary: Goldman and Berkman spent the Jewish New Year with Dr. Landesman's family in Odessa. Berkman suffered a stomach attack during the meal and was diagnosed with an ulcerated stomach.

citation.quote: No doubt we knew, the doctor said, that Rosh Hashona was at hand, and he would be happy to have us celebrate the great day together in the company of his family.

title: Robbery on the expedition train
summary: Returning toward Petrograd, thieves robbed Berkman's compartment of his clothes, a Browning pistol, a gold watch, and sixteen hundred dollars representing the couple's entire savings from American friends.

citation.quote: Early in the morning Shakol and I were torn out of sleep by someone knocking on our door. Still dazed, we heard Sasha's voice demanding to know why we had played such a fool hoax on him.

title: Expedition journeys to Archangel
summary: Goldman and Berkman traveled north to Archangel, where they found temperatures of fifty below zero but a Soviet administration notable for its respect for human life, even toward former White officers, nuns, and monks.

citation.quote: Archangel, at the mouth of the northern Dvina, was separated from the railroad terminus by the frozen river. On arriving we found a temperature of fifty below zero, but the brilliant sun and the dry, crisp air made the cold far less penetrating than in Petrograd.

title: Founding of the American Civil Liberties Union
summary: The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) was founded; lawyer Gilbert Roe served as one of its early advisers.

citation.quote: Gilbert Roe (1865-1929): lawyer and author; adviser to the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) after its founding in 1920.

title: John Reed dies in Moscow
summary: John Reed died of typhus in Moscow while working in the Soviet bureau of propaganda. Honored by the Soviets, he was buried in the Kremlin wall.

citation.quote: John Reed (1887-1920): journalist and political radical... Reed worked in the Soviet bureau of propaganda and died in Moscow of typhus. Honored by the Soviets, he was buried in the Kremlin wall.

title: Radek elected to Bolshevik Central Committee
summary: German socialist and Russian Bolshevik Karl Radek was elected to the Bolshevik Central Committee.

citation.quote: Karl Radek (1885-1939): German socialist, Russian Bolshevik, and Trotskyist journalist. Elected to the Bolshevik Central Committee in 1920, he was expelled from the party after Lenin's death and purged by Stalin in 1937.

title: Tomsky leads Red International Trade Union
summary: Russian socialist and trade union organizer Mikhail Tomsky led the Red International Trade Union.

citation.quote: Mikhail Tomsky (1880-1936): a Russian socialist and trade union organizer who led the Red International Trade Union in 1920.

title: Goldman and Berkman arrive in Soviet Russia
summary: After deportation from the United States aboard the Buford, Goldman and Berkman crossed the Soviet border and reached Petrograd, where they were welcomed by workers, soldiers, and Bolshevik officials.

citation.quote: At the border, on our way to Petrograd, and at the station there, we were received like dear comrades. We who had been driven out of America as felons were welcomed on Soviet soil as brothers by her sons and daughters who had helped to set her free.

title: Reunion with Bill Shatoff in Petrograd
summary: Days after arrival, Goldman and Berkman were reunited with their old comrade Bill Shatoff, who had become a Bolshevik official. He spent two weeks with them recounting the Revolution before leaving for Siberia.

citation.quote: In the hotel corridor we ran into a young woman who told us that she was on her way to the Zorins' to call us. A friend from America was waiting, eager to see us. We followed her to an apartment on the fourth floor, and when the door was opened, I found myself in the embrace of our old comrade Bill Shatoff.

title: Secret anarchist conference in Petrograd
summary: Goldman attended a clandestine gathering of Petrograd anarchists who denounced Bolshevik persecution, raids on anarchist headquarters, mass executions, and the emasculation of the soviets.

citation.quote: Soon, however, other voices rose from the depths, harsh, accusing voices that greatly disturbed me. I had been asked to attend a conference of anarchists in Petrograd, and I was amazed to find that my comrades were compelled to gather in secret in an obscure hiding-place.

title: Buford reaches the English Channel
summary: The deportation ship Buford reached the English Channel, where the mail-bag carried away by the pilot contained the deportees' first letters back to the United States.

citation.quote: It was January 5, 1920, when we reached the English Channel. The mail-bag carried away by the pilot contained our first letters to the United States.

title: George Lansbury and Barry visit Petrograd
summary: British Daily Herald editor George Lansbury and American correspondent Barry arrived unexpectedly in Petrograd. Berkman, recovering from illness, accompanied them to Moscow as interpreter.

citation.quote: About this time two men were sent up to see us: George Lansbury, editor of the London Daily Herald, and Mr. Barry, an American correspondent. They had not been expected and no provision had been made for an English-speaking person to meet them.

title: John Reed visits Goldman in Petrograd
summary: Journalist John Reed visited Goldman before departing for America by way of Latvia. Their conversation revealed Reed's hardened defense of Bolshevik executions, which shocked Goldman.

citation.quote: John Reed had burst into my room like a sudden ray of light, the old buoyant, adventurous Jack that I used to know in the States. He was about to return to America, by way of Latvia.

title: Goldman travels by train to Moscow
summary: After ten days of awaiting permits, Goldman traveled to Moscow on a train with Karl Radek, Maxim Gorki, and the poet Demyan Bedny. She had a long conversation with Gorki en route.

citation.quote: Arrived at the station, I found myself in distinguished company. Karl Radek, who had escaped the fate of Liebknecht, Rosa Luxemburg, and Landauer, was there. Chiperovich, head of the Petrograd labour unions, Maxim Gorki, and several lesser lights were also in the same car with me.

title: Goldman meets Alexandra Kollontay in Moscow
summary: Goldman sought out Alexandra Kollontay at the Hotel National in Moscow. Kollontay dismissed Goldman's concerns about Bolshevik abuses as 'dull grey spots' and invited her to work among Russian women.

citation.quote: Alexandra Kollontay and Angelica Balabanoff were within easy reach, as they were living in the National. I sought out the former first. Mme Kollontay looked remarkably young and radiant, considering her fifty years and the severe operation she had recently undergone.

title: Goldman meets Anatol Lunacharsky in the Kremlin
summary: Two days after meeting Kollontay, Goldman visited the People's Commissar for Education in the Kremlin. Lunacharsky offered her work on educational reform and discussed his disputes with conservative instructors.

citation.quote: Two days later I went to see Anatol Lunacharsky. His quarters were in the Kremlin, the impenetrable citadel of authority in the popular mind of Russia.

title: Goldman meets Angelica Balabanoff
summary: Goldman visited Angelica Balabanoff in the Hotel National. Balabanoff, ill and disillusioned with the Bolshevik bureaucracy, urged Goldman to seek out Lenin.

citation.quote: The two leading Communist women of Russia proved the greatest contrast. Angelica Balabanoff lacked what Kollontay possessed in abundance: the latter's fine figure, good looks, and youthful litheness, as well as her worldly polish and sophistication.

title: Goldman and Berkman interview Lenin in the Kremlin
summary: Lenin received Goldman and Berkman in his Kremlin office. He dismissed their concerns about imprisoned anarchists, claimed only bandits and Makhnovists were jailed, and proposed they organize a Russian Friends of American Freedom society.

citation.quote: Lenin's auto rushed at furious speed along the congested streets and into the Kremlin, past every sentry without being halted for propusks. At the entrance of one of the ancient buildings that stood apart from the rest, we were asked to alight.

title: Goldman and Berkman first visit Kropotkin in Dmitrov
summary: Goldman and Berkman traveled by special train with Lansbury and Barry to Dmitrov, where they found Peter Kropotkin ill, gaunt, and living in a poorly heated room with his wife Sophie and daughter Alexandra.

citation.quote: The train crawled snail-like, stopping at every water-tank. It was late evening when we at last reached the house. We found Peter ill and worn-looking. He appeared a mere shadow of the sturdy man I had known in Paris and London in 1907.

title: Goldman and Berkman join Museum of the Revolution
summary: Goldman and Berkman visited the Museum of the Revolution at the Winter Palace and agreed to join its staff under secretary M. B. Kaplan, charged with collecting documents of the Russian revolutionary movement.

citation.quote: We were received by the secretary, M. B. Kaplan, a man in the middle thirties, of pleasant and intelligent appearance. \[ ... \] Though it was the latter part of May, the vast chambers of the Winter Palace were breathing a penetrating chill.

title: Museum Expedition train departs Petrograd
summary: After seven months in Soviet Russia, Goldman and Berkman's renovated railway car was attached to the night train 'Maxim Gorki' to begin the Museum of the Revolution's expedition to collect historical documents across the country.

citation.quote: On June 30, 1920, just seven months after we had landed on Soviet soil, our renovated car was hitched to a night train, known as 'Maxim Gorki,' and headed for Moscow.

title: Second Congress of the Red Trade-Union International
summary: Foreign delegates of the Second Congress of the Red Trade-Union International arrived in Moscow, including anarcho-syndicalists from Spain, France, Italy, Germany, and Scandinavia. Goldman conferred with them about Russian conditions.

citation.quote: There was great excitement in the city, due to the arrival of a number of foreign delegates for the Second Congress of the Red Trade-Union International. Among them we were delighted to find some Anarcho-Syndicalists from Spain, France, Italy, Germany, and Scandinavia.

title: Expedition reaches Kharkov
summary: The Museum Expedition arrived in Kharkov, which appeared prosperous after Petrograd and Moscow. They documented Ukrainian Communist hostility toward Moscow's central authority and encountered a Russian engineer who described persecution in the Don basin.

citation.quote: Our first important stop was at Kharkov. It looked prosperous after Petrograd and Moscow. The people, fine physical types of humanity, appeared well fed and carefree in spite of the numerous invasions, changes of government, and the ravages the city had experienced.

title: Second visit to Kropotkin in Dmitrov
summary: On their summer visit, Goldman and Berkman found Kropotkin in good health and high spirits, proudly showing them Sophie's vegetable garden. He warned them that syndicalism would be needed to organize future revolutions.

citation.quote: The shock was the greater because we had visited Peter in July and had found him in good health and buoyant spirits. He seemed then younger and better than when we had seen him the previous March.

title: Death of John Reed in Moscow
summary: Goldman read in a Soviet newspaper of John Reed's death from typhus. Reed had contracted the disease at the Congress of Eastern Races in Baku, after being sent there by Zinoviev despite his weakened condition.

citation.quote: Sad news clouded our joy. In a Soviet paper we read of the death of John Reed. Both Sasha and I had been very fond of Jack and we felt his demise as a personal loss.

title: John Reed's funeral in Red Square
summary: John Reed was buried in Red Square with artificial wreaths and a grey, drizzly sky. Alexandra Kollontay gave a beautiful tribute. Louise Bryant collapsed as the coffin was lowered.

citation.quote: A grey sky overhanging Moscow, rain steadily drizzling its melancholy tune, and artificial wreaths that had served at other funerals were Jack Reed's farewell in the Red Square. No beauty for the man who had loved it so, no colour for his artist-soul.

title: Rout of General Wrangel
summary: While stopped at Bryansk, the expedition learned of the complete rout of General Wrangel's White army, with Nestor Makhno credited for helping bring about the victory after the Bolsheviks had previously denounced him as a bandit.

citation.quote: In Bryansk we were greeted with the joyful news of the complete rout of Wrangel. Strange to say, Nestor Makhno was being proclaimed a hero who had materially helped to bring about the great victory.

title: Christmas Eve on the snowbound expedition train
summary: Stalled by a blizzard fifty miles from Petrograd on the return from Archangel, Shakol and Berkman surprised Goldman with a small decorated pine tree, candles, and a hot grog made from rum supplied in Archangel.

citation.quote: On Christmas Eve, still held up on the road, Shakol and Sasha gave me a surprise. A wee pine-tree, decorated for the occasion and studded with coloured candles, gaily lit up our compartment.

title: Big Bill Haywood flees to the Soviet Union
summary: American radical labor organizer William "Big Bill" Haywood, founding member of the IWW, fled to the Soviet Union after being convicted of violating the Espionage and Sedition Acts.

citation.quote: William "Big Bill" Haywood (1869-1928): American radical labor organizer, founding member of the Western Federation of Miners and the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW or the "Wobblies"). Convicted of violating Espionage and Sedition Acts, he fled to the Soviet Union in 1921.

title: Mollie Steimer deported to Russia
summary: Russian American anarchist Mollie Steimer, who had been imprisoned for distributing pamphlets opposing American intervention in the Russian revolution, was deported to Russia where she was subsequently imprisoned as an anarchist.

citation.quote: Mollie Steimer (1897-1980): a young Russian American anarchist who was imprisoned for distributing pamphlets opposing American intervention in the Russian revolution... Steimer was deported to Russia in 1921 where she was subsequently imprisoned as an anarchist.

title: Branting serves as prime minister of Sweden
summary: Hjalmar Branting, called "the father of socialism" in Sweden, served as prime minister in 1921 (and again in 1924).

citation.quote: Hjalmar Branting (1860-1925): called "the father of socialism" in Sweden, served as prime minister in 1921 and 1924.

title: Kropotkin's funeral in Moscow
summary: Tens of thousands marched in Kropotkin's two-hour funeral procession from the Trade Union House to the Devichy Cemetery. The Cheka briefly released seven anarchist prisoners to act as honorary pallbearers after threats to denounce the breach of Lenin's promise.

citation.quote: In Moscow the expressions of esteem and affection for Peter Kropotkin became a tremendous demonstration. From the moment the body arrived in the capital and was placed in the Trade Union House, and all during the two days that the dead lay in state in the Marble Hall, there began an outpouring of the people such as had not been manifested since the days of 'October.'

title: Kropotkin Memorial Committee formed
summary: Sophie Kropotkin proposed a Peter Kropotkin museum as a memorial. The Funeral Commission reorganized as a Memorial Committee, with Sophie as chairman, Berkman as general secretary, and Goldman as manager.

citation.quote: The Peter Kropotkin Funeral Commission reorganized itself into a Memorial Committee, with Sophie Kropotkin as its chairman, Sasha as general secretary, and me as manager.

title: Petrograd strike wave begins at Troubetskoy works
summary: Within twenty-four hours of Goldman's return to Petrograd, the city was seething with strikes. The Troubetskoy millmen struck for increased rations and footgear; five more factories joined, including the Galernaya docks, Admiralty shops, Patronny mills, Baltiysky and Laferm works.

citation.quote: The storm broke out even before anyone expected it. It began with the strike of the millmen at the Troubetskoy works. Their demands were modest enough: an increase in their food rations, as had long ago been promised them, and also the distribution of the foot-gear on hand.

title: Death of Peter Kropotkin
summary: Peter Kropotkin died of pneumonia at his home in Dmitrov at four in the morning. Goldman arrived from Petrograd hours too late after her train was delayed by a storm. He had reportedly asked for her in his final hours.

citation.quote: I hastened to the Kropotkin cottage. Alas, too late! Peter had ceased breathing an hour before. He died at four a.m., February 8, 1921.

title: Lenin and Trotsky denounce Kronstadt as mutiny
summary: Within an hour of news of the Kronstadt resolution, an order signed by Lenin and Trotsky declared the sailors had mutinied and labeled them tools of tsarist generals in a counter-revolutionary conspiracy.

citation.quote: An order signed by Lenin and Trotsky spread like wildfire through Petrograd. It declared that Kronstadt had mutinied against the Soviet Government, and denounced the sailors as 'tools of former tsarist generals who together with Socialist-Revolutionist traitors staged a counter-revolutionary conspiracy against the proletarian Republic.'

title: Petro-Soviet special session on Kronstadt
summary: Goldman and Berkman attended the Petro-Soviet session where Zinoviev's resolution demanding Kronstadt's immediate surrender on pain of extermination was rushed through. A striking arsenal worker and a sailor were shouted down attempting to defend the Kronstadters.

citation.quote: Unfortunately Trotsky's train was delayed and he failed to appear at the session. The men who addressed the gathering were beyond reason or appeal. Fanaticism run mad was in their words, and blind fear in their hearts.

title: Trotsky's ultimatum to Kronstadt
summary: On the same day as Goldman's appeal, Trotsky issued his ultimatum threatening to shoot the Kronstadt sailors 'like pheasants.' Signed by Trotsky and Kamenev as Commander-in-Chief of the Red Army, it demanded unconditional surrender.

citation.quote: Proof that our appeal had fallen on deaf ears came to us the very same day on the arrival of Trotsky and his ultimatum to Kronstadt. By order of the Workers' and Peasants' Government, he declared to the Kronstadt sailors and soldiers, he would 'shoot like pheasants' all those who had dared to 'raise their hand against the Socialist fatherland.'

title: Bolshevik suppression of the Kronstadt rebellion
summary: For ten days the Bolsheviks under Trotsky and Tukhachevsky bombarded Kronstadt with artillery and aerial bombs, eventually storming the fortress across the frozen Finnish Gulf with troops camouflaged in white shrouds.

citation.quote: During ten harrowing days and nights the sailors and workers of the besieged city held out against a continuous artillery fire from three sides and bombs hurled from aeroplanes upon the non-combatant community. Heroically they repulsed the repeated attempts of the Bolsheviki to storm the fortresses by special troops from Moscow.

title: Kronstadt mass meeting adopts Petropavlovsk resolution
summary: Sixteen thousand sailors, Red Army men, and workers at Kronstadt unanimously adopted resolutions of solidarity with the striking Petrograd workers, demanding freedom of assembly for unions and the release of political prisoners. Only Vassiliev, Kuzmin, and Kalinin opposed.

citation.quote: At an open-air meeting on March I, attended by sixteen thousand sailors, Red Army men, and workers of Kronstadt, similar resolutions were adopted unanimously with the exception of only three votes. The dissenters included Vassiliev, president of the Kronstadt Soviet, who was chairman of the mass meeting; Kuzmin, the Commissar of the Baltic Fleet; and Kalinin, President of the Federated Socialist Soviet Republics.

title: Goldman and Berkman appeal to Zinoviev on Kronstadt
summary: Goldman, Berkman, Perkus, and Petrovsky sent a letter to the Petrograd Soviet of Labour and Defence chaired by Zinoviev, urging that the Kronstadt dispute be settled by a five-person commission, two of them anarchists, rather than by force of arms.

citation.quote: Petrograd ALEXANDER BERKMAN March 5, 1921 EMMA GOLDMAN

title: Goldman spends Christmas in Latvian jail
summary: [Inference] While detained in Latvia after being arrested on the train from Riga, Goldman prepared a Christmas feast for fellow prisoners with help from a sympathetic guard, the day after an official told her her detention was 'an unfortunate mistake.'

citation.quote: The guard did my Christmas shopping for me, bringing me fruit, nuts, cake, coffee, and a can of evaporated milk. Luxuries they were, but I was anxious to prepare a Christmas feast for my friends in the adjoining cells.

title: Frank Harris publishes My Life and Loves
summary: Journalist and author Frank Harris published his sensational autobiography, My Life and Loves.

citation.quote: Frank Harris (1856-1931): journalist and author who wrote a sensational autobiography, My Life and Loves (1922).

title: Peggy Guggenheim marries Lawrence Vail
summary: Patron of the arts Peggy Guggenheim married Lawrence Vail, an American writer.

citation.quote: Peggy Guggenheim (1898-1979): a patron of the arts, she married Lawrence Vail, an American writer, in 1922.

title: Tomsky elected to Central Committee of Communist Party
summary: Mikhail Tomsky was elected to the Central Committee of the Communist Party and later became a member of the Politburo before being purged by Stalin.

citation.quote: Elected to the Central Committee of the Communist Party in 1922 and later a member of the Politburo, Tomsky was purged by Stalin and committed suicide.

title: Goldman departs Reval, Estonia for Stockholm
summary: After being released from Latvian detention, Goldman and her companions departed Reval, Estonia, en route to Stockholm, Sweden, having obtained Swedish visas through syndicalist comrades.

citation.quote: At last, on January 2, 1922, we departed from Reval, Esthonia. To avoid a repetition of our Riga adventure we went directly to the steamer, though the boat was not to leave until the following morning.

title: Goldman's fifty-fourth birthday celebrated in Liebenstein
summary: Goldman's family arranged a surprise party for her fifty-fourth birthday in Liebenstein, where Henry Alsberg teased her as 'Queen E.G. and her court.'

citation.quote: "Queen E.G. and her court," teased Henry [Alsberg] at the lovely surprise party my family arranged for my fifty-fourth birthday.

title: My Disillusionment in Russia published with missing chapters
summary: Doubleday, Page and Company released Goldman's book under the unauthorized title 'My Disillusionment in Russia,' omitting the last twelve chapters including her crucial Afterword.

citation.quote: A copy of my book arrived with the last twelve chapters missing and with an entirely wrong title. As printed, the volume was an unfinished work, because the last chapters and particularly my Afterword, which represented the culminating essence of the whole, were left out.

title: My Two Years in Russia sold to Doubleday, Page and Company
summary: Harry Weinberger sent Goldman word that her manuscript had been sold by Brainard to Doubleday, Page and Company, with publication scheduled for October 1923.

citation.quote: It brought the good news that my manuscript had been sold by Brainard to Doubleday, Page and Company and that the book would be out in October of that year (1923).

title: Balabanoff emigrates from Russia
summary: Angelica Balabanoff emigrated from Russia as an anti-Bolshevik.

citation.quote: Elected secretary at the First International Congress in 1919, she emigrated from Russia in 1924 as an anti-Bolshevik.

title: Goldman leaves Germany for England
summary: After receiving a British visa secured with help from Frank Harris, Goldman departed Germany via Holland and France for England, hoping for asylum and a platform for her work.

citation.quote: With this thought to give me courage, I left Germany on July 24, 1924, via Holland and France, for England.

title: Trotsky expelled by Stalin
summary: Leon Trotsky, the first commissar of foreign affairs for the Soviet government under Lenin, was expelled by Stalin.

citation.quote: He was the first commissar of foreign affairs for the Soviet government under Lenin. Expelled by Stalin in 1926, he was assassinated by Stalin's agents in Mexico.

title: Goldman delivers final talk in Toronto lecture series
summary: In Toronto, Goldman delivered the last of a series of twenty lectures, with the final evening discussing Ben Lindsey's Companionate Marriage drawing an audience equal to four other meetings combined.

citation.quote: In January 1928 I delivered my final talk in a series of twenty, embracing various problems of our time. The last evening, on which I discussed Ben Lindsey's Companionate Marriage, brought out an audience equalling the total attendance of four other meetings.

title: Litvinov serves as Soviet Commissar for Foreign Affairs
summary: Maksim M. Litvinov, nominally subordinate to Chicherin, became People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs.

citation.quote: Maksim M. Litvinov nominally subordinate to Chicerin, became People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs during 1930-39 (see LML, 1970, 923).

title: Mayor LaGuardia closes Blackwell's Island Penitentiary
summary: Reform mayor LaGuardia closed Blackwell's Island Penitentiary; all inmates were moved to the new Rikers Island.

citation.quote: Blackwell's was closed by reform mayor LaGuardia in 1934. All inmates were moved to the new Rikers Island.

title: Agnes Smedley reports from China
summary: Journalist Agnes Smedley gained national prominence for reports from China.

citation.quote: Agnes Smedley (1892-1950): journalist and author who was active in the Indian independence movement. She gained national prominence for reports from China in 1936.

title: Karl Radek purged by Stalin
summary: Karl Radek was purged by Stalin after having been expelled from the Bolshevik party following Lenin's death.

citation.quote: Elected to the Bolshevik Central Committee in 1920, he was expelled from the party after Lenin's death and purged by Stalin in 1937.

title: Trotsky assassinated in Mexico
summary: Leon Trotsky was assassinated by Stalin's agents in Mexico.

citation.quote: Leon Trotsky (born Lev Davidovich Bronstein) (1879-1940): Russian Jewish revolutionary...

title: Kerensky moves to the United States
summary: Former Russian provisional government prime minister Alexander Kerensky moved to the United States and taught at American universities.

citation.quote: He moved to the United States in 1940 and taught at American universities.

title: Margaret Sanger founds Planned Parenthood
summary: American nurse and birth control pioneer Margaret Sanger founded Planned Parenthood.

citation.quote: Margaret Sanger (1879-1966): American nurse and pioneer of birth control movement; she founded Planned Parenthood in 1942.

title: Elizabeth Gurley Flynn imprisoned under the Smith Act
summary: Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, American Communist and IWW labor organizer, was imprisoned after conviction of conspiracy under the Smith Act.

citation.quote: Elizabeth Gurley Flynn (1890-1964): American socialist, feminist, and Communist; a lecturer and labor organizer for the IWW. Imprisoned after conviction of conspiracy under the Smith Act in 1952, she immigrated to and died in the Soviet Union.
